articles.title_orig: Putin, Trump and Xi Could Meet in China Next Month in High-Stakes Three-Way Summit
articles.title_zh: Putin, Trump and Xi Could Meet in China Next Month in High-Stakes Three-Way Summit
articles.content_orig:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has reportedly floated a three-way summit between himself, U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine, without Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the table.
The meeting was mentioned in a phone call to Trump on Oct. 9, the Wall Street Journal reported on Monday, citing a former Russian intelligence officer briefed on the matter. Such a summit may take place at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in November in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, according to the report.
The call also produced a deal for Moscow to sell diesel on the global market.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said early Monday that "there's been talks of a meeting. I don't know whether it's been finalized, but the president has been clear," he said in comments reported by Reuters.
"The president is open to anything that he can do to help bring a war to an end, if it's possible, and we'll continue to look for opportunities to do that," Rubio told reporters during a visit to Uzbekistan.
It comes amid mounting tensions between Ukraine and the U.S., its largest military backer. Over the past week, a series of moves by the Trump administration has raised fresh questions about Washington's reliability as Kyiv's most important military partner. It caused alarm among European allies and prompted criticism from fellow Republicans.
Over the weekend, Trump defended his decision to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports, as well as an executive order on Oct. 18 to waive new Russia sanctions from a bill introduced by the late Senator Lindsey Graham.
Trump and Zelenskyy have traded criticism over how to end the war in Ukraine, with Trump accusing the Ukrainian president of not wanting peace , while Zelenskyy has argued that Washington's easing of sanctions on Russia risks prolonging the conflict. In a post on X, Zelenskyy said that ″the decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me."
The tensions come as Russia launched another wave of overnight attacks on Ukraine, firing 16 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and the surrounding region and more than 200 drones across the country, according to Zelenskyy.
In a post on X on Monday, Zelenskyy said the strikes damaged more than 10 energy infrastructure facilities, leaving at least 550,000 households without power. He also said Ukraine had once again received no advance warning from its partners about the missile attacks. Casualties were reported, while a medical clinic, school, metro station and residential buildings were also damaged.
Ukraine's First Deputy Minister for Recovery, Infrastructure and Transport Serhiy Derkach told CNBC on Monday that Kyiv still hoped to retain Washington's support despite the growing tensions.
Asked whether the Trump administration was abandoning Ukraine and siding with Russia, Derkach said he did not believe the U.S. was abandoning Kyiv, but stressed that Ukraine hoped Washington would continue helping it or at least "stay in the middle."
"That's most important for us actually, not to lose the support of the U.S.," he said.
Russia has also intensified attacks on Ukraine's transport infrastructure, including road border crossings, railways and shipping routes, Derkach said.
It comes after Trump told Ukraine to stop striking Russian energy infrastructure, claiming that it was driving up global diesel prices.
Despite an "energy ceasefire" announced by Trump on Oct. 11, Russia continued striking Ukrainian infrastructure. Kyiv paused its attacks for three days before resuming them last Thursday, citing continued Russian strikes.
"America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements. On the contrary, they take every signal of an opportunity to make money as proof that their bet on war is paying off and they can keep fighting," the Ukrainian president wrote on Sunday.
On Sunday, he also told Bloomberg that "steps have been taken to convince Ukraine to capitulate."
"I am not saying that this is the goal our partners are pursuing. I don't want to think that our American partners believe the war" against Russia "could be ended sooner at Ukraine's expense. But that's how it looks."
Over the weekend, both Kyiv and Moscow traded strikes, with Ukraine launching a strike of over 1,000 drones into Russia, setting fires at an oil export terminal and refinery in the city of St. Petersburg, while Moscow pounded Kyiv with ballistic missiles.
Last week, Kyiv also accused Washington of ordering restrictions on its Starshield networks, the military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink. Ukraine relies on this connectivity to track and intercept incoming threats.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk pinned responsibility for any restrictions on the U.S. government and Trump, writing on X that "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government."
Trump denied on Friday that the White House had ordered restrictions on Starlink satellite internet services provided to Ukraine's armed forces, after Reuters reported on Thursday that the call to restrict Starlink in Ukraine came from someone inside the White House, citing two U.S. officials.
The Telegraph reported on Friday that Musk "approached Donald Trump with the idea of slowing down Starlink in Ukraine," and both had a hand in imposing the restrictions.
Additionally, Zelenskyy told NBC's Meet the Press on Sunday that intelligence sharing between the two countries had been interrupted, but later "de-blocked."
Rubio on Monday denied that Washington had suspended intelligence sharing with Ukraine, contradicting Zelenskyy's claim that the flow of information had been briefly interrupted, Reuters reported.
Speaking to reporters in Uzbekistan, Rubio insisted there had been no pause and said Zelenskyy should instead focus on ending the war, marking another public disagreement between Washington and Kyiv amid deteriorating relations.
— CNBC's Lora Kolodny contributed to this report.

Ricardo Gonzalez was injured and taken to hospital after confrontation in Long Beach, according to officials
Federal immigration agents broke the arm of a US citizen in what a Democratic congressman said was a “brutal attack” during a confrontation with protesters in California.
Video of Saturday’s encounter in Long Beach shows Ricardo Gonzalez, identified as a former city employee, handcuffed and face down in a gutter, with Immigration and Customs Enforcement ( ICE ) officers kneeling on his back.
Rex Richardson, Long Beach’s mayor, told CNN on Sunday that Gonzalez had called emergency responders for help at one point. In an online fundraiser for his medical expenses, Gonzalez’s daughter, Leslie, said he was knocked off his e-bike by an unmarked ICE vehicle.
“He was tased twice, pinned to the ground, and taken to the hospital for serious injuries,” Leslie’s fundraiser said. “What ICE did was not right.”
Richardson said: “When the police arrived, we know that he was detained. He was on a curb. He was injured.”
The episode centering on Gonzalez is the latest in a number of recent violent and sometimes deadly encounters involving federal officers conducting enforcement actions as part of Donald trump’s immigration crackdown.
The homeland security department, which oversees ICE, has not commented publicly on why Gonzalez was detained. But it frequently portrays its agents’ actions as self-defense or protecting public safety.
The Guardian has contacted ICE for comment.
Congressman Robert Garcia, a Democrat who represents Long Beach, posted on X that he was disturbed by the encounter and called for the abolition of ICE.
“ICE agents brutally attacked and broke the arm of a North Long Beach resident and US citizen,” he wrote.
“The videos are horrific and should concern not just our community but the country. I’m proud of the neighbors who documented and stood up for the family being terrorized by ICE.
“Donald Trump and his inhumane and illegal deportation machine must be stopped. Long Beach stands with our community and our immigrant families.”
In a statement , the Long Beach police department (LBPD) said ICE personnel also called for emergency assistance “due to vehicle vandalism taking place and a subject in need of medical aid”. The LBPD statement also said officers arrived to find “a large group disturbance” taking place involving the federal agents.
“One officer located a handcuffed male adult, being detained by ICE, who was bleeding,” the statement said. “Officers transported the handcuffed injured man to a nearby fire station. There, LBPD personnel removed the handcuffs and LBFD personnel transported the man to the hospital for medical attention.”
The LBPD said it was not involved in any immigration enforcement action and made no arrests. It said ICE agents who followed officers into a secure parking lot “were subsequently directed to leave the station”.
“They were later advised that if they wanted to file a vandalism report, they could contact the City of Long Beach Communications Center,” the LBPD statement added.
The Gonzalez case in Long Beach has parallels with an incident in Texas on 10 October in which an ICE agent driving an unmarked SUV ran over a man and broke his leg in three places .
Harris county, Texas, district attorney Sean Teare said he was considering bringing felony assault charges against the immigration officer after video appeared to show the vehicle swerving into the man in a parking lot in the Houston area.
At a news conference on Friday, Houston-based advocacy group FIEL accused ICE of crashing into that man while searching for another who had died years earlier. A FIEL official told the Associated Press it had turned over to Teare a death certificate for the man the group says ICE was apparently looking for.
ICE on Friday did not respond to AP’s questions about the matter.

articles.title_orig: 3 waves of Russian missiles slam Kyiv overnight, killing at least 1, injuring 8
articles.title_zh: 3 waves of Russian missiles slam Kyiv overnight, killing at least 1, injuring 8
articles.content_orig:
Metro workers repair tracks damaged in a Russian attack in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Oct. 19, 2026. (Chris Occhicone/The Kyiv Independent)
Editor's note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
At least one person was killed and eight others injured after multiple waves of Russian missiles struck Kyiv overnight on Oct. 19.
Several explosions rocked the capital just before 11 p.m., with further attacks around 3 a.m. and 7 a.m., Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground reported. Ukraine's State Emergency Service (DSNS) said damage was reported in at least three districts.
One person was killed in the Desnianskyi District where a non-residential building caught fire and a metro station was damaged, DSNS said. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko earlier reported a fatality was that of 21-year-old woman.
The above-ground Chernihivska and Lisova metro stations were temporarily closed for repairs, city officials said.
Later on Oct. 19, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said more than 70 workers were repairing the damaged metro infrastructure, with the most difficult work involving power supply and train control systems. Repairs had continued since overnight but were being slowed by air raid alerts, which forced crews to take shelter.
Train service between Lisova and Akademmistechko stations was expected to resume that evening, with trains skipping Chernihivska until repairs were completed, Klitschko added.
Five people were injured in the Solomianskyi District when a 25-story residential building was damaged, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported. It is not yet clear where the other injuries occurred.
Допис, поширений Kyiv Independent (@kyivindependent_official)
The Cosmo Multimall shopping and entertainment center sustained significant damage in the Solomianskyi District. Its administration said no employees were injured and that the mall was working to resume operations as soon as possible. The center did not disclose the extent of the damage or provide a timeline for repairs.
Serhii Misan, 68, a local resident, had planned to pick up his new refrigerator from Cosmo Multimall on the morning of Oct. 19.
"I only paid for a refrigerator yesterday, and they told me I could pick it up today," Misan said. "And now look at what's happening here."
"(The Russians) are terrorists. They strike civilian targets. They spare no one — not children, not equipment, no one. They just kill civilians."
Misan added that, in light of recent developments, Ukraine would struggle to resist Russia without a strong partner like the U.S.
"If aid is reduced, it will be very difficult to stand up to an aggressor like Russia," he said. "We are not trying to seize their land. We are trying to defend our right to live freely on our own land."
Sofiia Kelli, 18, who lives in the Solomianskyi district, told The Kyiv Independent that her apartment was also damaged in the Russian attack on the capital. Her family was only able to take shelter in an underground parking garage after the attack began, as there was too little time between the air raid alert and the strikes.
"It was a huge shock. It was extremely loud — nothing like the other explosions we've heard in our neighborhood," Kelli said.
"I couldn't fall asleep afterward. Then I just sat in the bathroom and cried for a very long time. It's hard to process everything that happened because you always think something like this won't happen to you. And then it does."
"They [Russians] strike civilian targets. They [Russians] spare no one — not children, not equipment, no one. They [Russians] just kill civilians."
Kelli said she intends to stay in Kyiv despite the latest attack and is getting ready for the coming winter.
"Everything depends on electricity. Of course, it's difficult, but we're doing the best we can. We've installed solar panels (on the building) and a generator to keep the elevators running," she added.
Klitschko also reported damage to a medical center in the same district. The blast wave shattered more than 200 windows, damaged doors and ceilings, and damaged medical equipment, he said.
No medical center staff were injured, and there were no patients inside the facility at the time of the attack.
The Russian attack also destroyed a data center operated by telecommunications company Datagroup, which provides electronic communications services to users in more than 90 settlements across Ukraine.
The company said the facility's equipment and infrastructure had been damaged beyond repair. No employees were injured in the attack.
Russian attacks also hit settlements in Kyiv Oblast surrounding the capital. In Irpin, about 20 kilometers (12 miles) northwest of Kyiv, one woman was killed and 19 people were injured, including nine children.
At around 9 a.m. local time, Tymur Tkachenko , head of the Kyiv Regional Military Administration, said that three people were missing. Search operations are ongoing, he added.
The Russian strikes damaged 70 houses, five apartment buildings, industrial facilities, and warehouses in Irpin, according to Tkachenko.
Recent ballistic missile strikes on Kyiv have arrived with little or no advance warning amid deteriorating relations between Ukraine and the U.S., which provides intelligence used to track Russian missile launches.
President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed on the morning of Oct. 19 that Russian forces had attacked Ukraine with ballistic missiles, adding that Kyiv had received no advance warning from its partners about the launches.
According to Zelensky, Russia fired 16 ballistic missiles, with Kyiv and the surrounding region being the primary targets.
"When deliveries of missiles for Ukraine's air defense are blocked while Russia is granted relief or delays in sanctions, this is, unfortunately, a denial of reality on the part of our partners," Zelensky wrote on X.
"The reality is that the war continues, and it continues solely because of Russian strikes and Russia's desire to drag this war out."
Yurii Ihnat, head of the Ukrainian Air Force's communications department, said on national television that Russia launched two waves of ballistic missile attacks overnight on Oct. 19, at around 11 p.m. and 3 a.m. local time.
Ukraine received no advance warning from its partners ahead of the first wave, but information about the second wave was provided, Ihnat said.
He added that a similar situation had occurred during previous attacks, including the one overnight on Oct. 14.
"Information was indeed not provided the first time, for certain reasons. Our experts are looking into this together with our partners, as this is not the first time such a situation has occurred. Information was provided at 3 a.m.," Ihnat said.
"The 'warning' about a ballistic threat came through only after the strike had already happened."
Commenting on Ukrainian officials' claims that partners had not provided advance warning of Russia's ballistic missile launches overnight, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters on the morning of Oct. 19 that he "did not know exactly" what had happened.
"I know a few nights ago there was a software problem involving (Ukrainian) early warning system," Rubio said.
"I know that EUCOM (U.S. European Command) had been involved in looking at, and that's the report they gave us back.  I can't comment on what happened last night," he added.

articles.title_orig: Saudi Arabia to postpone in-person ‘Davos in the desert’ event after Houthi attacks
articles.title_zh: Saudi Arabia to postpone in-person ‘Davos in the desert’ event after Houthi attacks
articles.content_orig:
Saudi Arabia has canceled in-person attendance at its flagship investment conference in Riyadh after Wall Street executives privately relayed safety concerns to organizers, including the boss of the kingdomâs sovereign wealth fund, people familiar with the matter said. Organizers of the Future Investment Initiative, due to take place next week, have dropped plans for a gathering of global and regional chief executives, and are telling delegates the event is postponed until 2027, the people said, confirming a Semafor story that a decision to postpone would be made today. The conference, which has become informally known as âDavos in the Desert,â is Saudi Arabiaâs highest profile event, attended by some of the biggest names in global finance and business. Next weekâs edition had been set to host JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon, Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon, and BlackRock CEO Larry Fink. Big banks and private equity firms had been privately relaying safety concerns about attending FII to Yasir Al-Rumayyan, Semafor reported earlier, according to people familiar with the matter.
Multiple signals suggested FII could be postponed: Rooms at the Ritz Carlton in Riyadh, which is usually blocked for the event, have been available for public booking in the past 24 hours. Other scheduled events such as an exhibition tennis tournament, a charity event linked to the crown prince, and Riyadh Fashion Week have all been postponed after the Houthis escalated attacks on the kingdom.
Delaying the conference is not surprising as the airport appears to still be closed, the main business district has instructed tenants to work from home until further notice, and schools have also shifted to home learning.
The kingdom, and its neighbors like the UAE and Qatar, have pitched themselves as not just sources of capital, but as a safe home for trillions in financial assets, data centers, and new industries.
Speculation has swirled in recent weeks over whether Saudi Arabia would go forward with the event, given high-profile attacks on the Riyadh airport. Organizers have held discussions around allowing overseas executives to participate virtually , Reuters reported last week, and The Wall Street Journal said that some executives had already canceled meetings .
The US, along with most other Western governments, recommends against all but essential travel to Saudi Arabia. That has knock-on effects on travel insurance costs and advice from internal security and risk teams.
Still, Saudi Arabia has viewed attendance at the event, and general support for the Gulf during turbulent times, as a loyalty test for global business leaders. Those who show up in tough times are rewarded, while fair-weather friends are often excluded from lucrative deals .
This story has been updated to reflect FIIâs decision to cancel the in-person meeting.

articles.title_orig: What's behind Egypt's move towards possible military involvement in Saudi-Yemen conflict?
articles.title_zh: What's behind Egypt's move towards possible military involvement in Saudi-Yemen conflict?
articles.content_orig:
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi has requested emergency parliamentary approval to defend Saudi Arabia against escalating attacks by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
The announcement follows military assistance from Pakistan and Turkey, which have deployed personnel, equipment and other defensive resources to support Saudi Arabia amid renewed fighting in Yemen.
Speaking at a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian Military Academy on Saturday , October 17, al-Sisi said Egypt was prepared to intervene if requested by Saudi Arabia, but stressed that any action would require parliamentary approval.
“I call on parliament to convene an emergency session to authorise us to take action to intervene in defence of Saudi Arabia, if we are asked to do so,” he said.
“This move and this defence require approval from the Egyptian parliament. I hope parliament will convene an emergency session to grant this authorisation.
"I am not speaking about attacking or waging war. We are seeking only to defend.”
Egypt's House of Representatives subsequently scheduled an emergency session for Sunday, October 18, in response to the president's request.
The announcement comes amid renewed missile and drone attacks by the Houthis on Saudi infrastructure, including Riyadh's international airport and facilities belonging to state oil company Saudi Aramco.
Fighting intensified after a truce in Yemen collapsed , with Saudi-backed forces launching a fresh campaign against the Houthis, who control significant territory in the country.
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi reaffirmed his country's commitment to defending Saudi Arabia, warning against threats to Red Sea security and international shipping lanes while stressing that Cairo would not stand aside if the kingdom faced further attacks.
"I want to tell the whole world that we are not looking for a role to play, but it is absolutely unacceptable for us to allow the kingdom of Saudi Arabia to be targeted or for its security and stability to be undermined," he added.
Egypt's announcement comes as Pakistan and Turkey strengthen defence cooperation with Saudi Arabia under the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, signed on August 7, 2026, which treats an armed attack against one member as an attack against all three.
Pakistan has deployed military personnel and resources to Saudi Arabia , with its Foreign Ministry confirming on October 9 that their role was defensive and did not involve operations inside Yemen.
Turkey has also provided air defence systems, intelligence support, drone operators and logistics, according to Reuters . President Recep Tayyip Erdogan announced on October 12 that he would submit the agreement to parliament for ratification.
Earlier in October, officials from the three countries met in Riyadh and agreed to coordinate military resources to strengthen Saudi Arabia's security against Houthi attacks.
Neither Pakistan nor Turkey has confirmed deploying combat troops into Yemen, with their reported assistance focused on defending Saudi territory.
The developments coincide with Egypt's consideration of joining the Mecca defence alliance, with Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty confirming on October 13 that Cairo was examining membership but had yet to make a final decision.

articles.title_zh: Amazon stock pops after Morgan Stanley details 5 catalysts, lifts price target
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Amazon ( AMZN ) stock rose more than 3% in early trading on Monday after Morgan Stanley named it a top pick and raised its price target to $350 from $335, outlining five catalysts that could drive the stock higher.
The new target implies about 40% upside from Friday's close of $250. With a bear case of $220 a share and a bull case of $410, the firm sees a 3:1 risk-reward ratio.
"In a market of see-sawing AI leaders and laggards, we detail 5 catalysts ahead to re-rate shares and drive material outperformance," analyst Brian Nowak, who kept his Overweight rating, wrote in a note Sunday.
Faster AWS growth: Morgan Stanley now expects revenue at AWS, Amazon's cloud unit, to grow 47% in 2027 and 42% in 2028, up from 41% and 37%. The change follows Nvidia's ( NVDA ) disclosure that it expects AWS to buy and deploy about 2 million of its GPUs over those two years. The extra chips also lift the firm's capital spending forecast for Amazon to $355 billion in 2027 and $365 billion in 2028.
Bigger AWS profits: Nowak expects AWS operating margins of 42% in 2027 and 44% in 2028, which supports about $16.50 in Amazon earnings per share in 2028.
Bedrock: More visibility into Bedrock, Amazon's AI model service, could lift the stock's valuation from about 15 times 2028 earnings, according to the note.
AI shopping: Nowak expects Amazon to emerge as a winner as AI shopping agents spread and expects it to partner over time with Meta's ( META ) Muse AI agent . The holiday season is the first big test.
Robotics: Every 10% of Amazon's global units that move through its robotics-enabled fulfillment centers could save $2 billion to $4 billion a year, Morgan Stanley estimates. The firm calls robotics a 2027 catalyst.
Amazon stock is up about 11% this year but sits roughly 10% below its early August high. Earlier this month, Yahoo Finance's Brian Sozzi noted that Amazon was trading at one of its lowest trailing price-to-earnings ratios in years . Morgan Stanley's $350 target is based on about 21 times its 2028 earnings estimate.
Amazon reports third quarter results on Oct. 29 after the bell.

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: Russian foreign minister says he's visiting Iran for talks to avert return to "large-scale war"
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Russian foreign minister says he's visiting Iran for talks to avert return to "large-scale war"
articles.content_orig:
Iran's top diplomat on Monday accused the United States of being responsible for the insecurity in the Strait of Hormuz that has left the nearly-eight month conflict sparked by joint U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran unresolved, despite the cessation of major military operations.
"The war imposed by the United States and the Zionist regime [Israel], combined with the economic blockade [on Iran's ports], constitutes the principal source of insecurity in our region," said Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, echoing many similar statements by himself and other senior Iranian figures.
He made the remark Monday during a joint news conference with his Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov, who arrived in Tehran earlier Monday for his first visit since the outbreak of the war, as Russia tries to frame itself as a potential mediator despite close ties with the Iranian regime.
Lavrov was also scheduled to meet Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian during his visit, according to Russia's foreign ministry. The veteran Russian diplomat said Moscow's efforts were "aimed at preventing the return of a large-scale war," with talks between Tehran and Washington at a standstill.
Iran's Acting Oil Minister Hamid Bovard met Qatar's Minister of State for Energy Affairs, Saad Sherida al-Kaabi, in Doha on Monday to discuss energy relations and cooperation between the two countries.
According to Iran's official news agency IRNA , al-Kaabi confirmed the meeting, which focused on bilateral energy ties and opportunities for cooperation.
The death toll from a Houthi missile strike on a camp in Yemen's government-controlled Shabwa province rose to 50 on Monday, a government official told the French news agency AFP, after military sources earlier put the toll at more than 30.
The Iran-backed rebels fired ballistic missiles at the al-Alam military camp in the southern province of Shabwa.
"The death toll has risen to at least 50, with more than 100 people injured, some of them in critical condition," said Fahad al-Khalifi, deputy governor of Shabwa.
He added that hospitals in the province were overwhelmed and had been forced to transfer the most seriously wounded to facilities in neighbouring Hadramout and Aden.
Iran-backed Houthi rebels struck a military camp for government forces in southern Yemen on Monday, killing at least 20 soldiers, two Yemeni military officials said.
The rebels fired ballistic missiles at the al-Alam military camp in the southern province of Shabwa in an attack that left at least two dozen more troops wounded, the officials said.
The military officials with the internationally recognized government of Yemen spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to brief the media.
Yemen's decade-long civil war has intensified and become intertwined with the wider regional conflict sparked by the U.S. war with Iran over the last few months, as the Houthis, considered one of Iran's most potent proxy forces, attacks the government's Saudi backers on their home turf.
Houthi strikes on Saudi infrastructure, including civilian airports, have killed more than 20 people in recent weeks, and President Trump has said he's considering joining Saudi operations against the rebels. The Houthis have warned that if the U.S. does intervene, it would prompt a  "swift and painful" retaliation against U.S. personnel and interests across the region.
Oil prices were down early Monday, with Brent crude, the international standard, falling 2.5% to $107.16 per barrel and benchmark U.S. crude dropping 2.2% to $96.84 per barrel.
The prices fell after President Trump late Friday signed an executive order to put new U.S. sanctions against Russia on hold just days before they were to come into effect, drawing disappointment from Ukraine , with the move likely resulting in more energy exports from Russia.
Mr. Trump's decision came not long after he said earlier this month he had reached a diesel deal with Russia in an attempt to bring down elevated U.S. fuel prices ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
But despite Mr. Trump's controversial efforts to ease energy costs for Americans, oil prices have remained much higher compared to before the Iran war, due in large part to the ongoing risks to the supply chain caused by the crisis in the Middle East .
On Friday the price of Brent crude hit nearly $110 a barrel, its highest level since mid-May.
A tug boat traveling near the Strait of Hormuz was struck by two unknown projectiles, a British maritime monitoring agency said Sunday .
The U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center (UKMTO) said in a statement that a tugboat traveling southbound off the coast of the United Arab Emirates "reported being struck by two unknown projectiles."
"The tug has sustained damage but is continuing on its route," the agency said, "one minor casualty has been reported."
Last week saw 10 attacks on commercial vessels in and near the strait, according to the UKMTO, which said October has already become the worst month for attacks on shipping in the strait since the early days of the war in March.

A Massachusetts company recalled more than 1.5 million pounds of ready-to-eat meat and poultry products that were produced over the past eight months after determining that they may not have been stored properly.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture posted the recall by Kayem Foods Inc., along with a list of scores of affected products. In addition to its own branded products, Kayem pulled items made under Al Fresco, McKenzie, and multiple other brands. (See lists below.)
The recalled products were manufactured over an eight-month span that stretches from March 31, 2026, to Oct. 7, 2026, and sent to stores and food service companies across the United States, as well as in Hong Kong, the statement on the USDA website indicated.
The affected items will have the establishment numbers "EST. M/P 7839," "EST. P 20935A" and "EST. M 9520" inside the USDA mark of inspection, it noted. See slideshow for images of the packaging of the recalled products.

The USDA website explained that the recall was triggered after a customer complained about a product being warm when it was delivered at the beginning of October. While the USDA is not aware of any illnesses linked to the products, its Food Safety and Inspection Service is concerned that the items may still be sitting in customers’ refrigerators. It advises anyone who finds one of the packages to throw it out or return it to its place of purchase.

articles.title_orig: 4 Cool New Features Your Fitbit Air Is Getting In October 2026
articles.title_zh: 4 Cool New Features Your Fitbit Air Is Getting In October 2026
articles.content_orig:
While the new Fitbit Edge is set to release in late October, the older Fitbit Air remains one of the best affordable fitness trackers you can buy today . It doesn't offer the same experience as a full smartwatch, but the Fitbit Air's comfortable build and versatile set of health and wellness tracking features make it a great alternative to Whoop and other screenless fitness bands.
While the Fitbit Air already comes with most features you'd want from a fitness tracker, Google recently announced several additions and improvements coming alongside the Fitbit Edge later in the month. These include the ability to passively track blood pressure trends, insulin resistance levels, and sleep breathing quality, which are all part of Google's new AI-based Health Guardian suite. Existing features like automatic workout detection are also being improved, and Google has also announced several partnerships with other health organizations to offer cross-platform compatibility with a variety of third-party services, devices, and apps. Some of these features are already rolling out, while users can expect others closer to the end of the month.
The American Heart Association labels hypertension (high blood pressure) as a 'silent killer' due to its lack of apparent symptoms until detected through screening. With nearly half of the adult population in the U.S. suffering from hypertension and being at risk of a heart attack or other health complications, monitoring blood pressure is extremely important — and Google is making it convenient for those with a Fitbit Air.
Google's new Health Guardian suite of features includes blood pressure trend tracking for users with a Google Health Premium subscription, which costs $9.99 monthly or $99.99 annually. This uses the watch's optical heart rate and motion sensors alongside Google's WavesFM AI model to passively measure your blood pressure trends throughout the day and warn you of any risks on the first of every month. Google states that this isn't meant to replace a dedicated blood pressure measuring device, but it provides a proactive way to notice changes without having to visit a doctor. It's also worth noting that neither the Fitbit Air nor Google Pixel watches support on-demand blood pressure readings.
Blood pressure monitoring is nothing new in the wearable space. The 2021 Huawei Watch D offered background blood pressure tracking and on-demand measurements using a mechanical pump built into the watch, and U.S. owners of select Samsung Galaxy watches, such as the Galaxy Watch 9 (with an external pump), and owners of Apple wearables like the Apple Watch Series 12 also got the feature earlier this year. Google Pixel watches and the Fitbit Air were a notable exception until now.
Another frequently undetected condition that can pose severe risks is insulin resistance or impaired insulin sensitivity. Insulin regulates blood sugar by aiding cells in the absorption of glucose to produce energy, and consistent resistance to it can lead to conditions like prediabetes and Type 2 diabetes, as well as other health complications.
Google is adding insulin resistance monitoring to the Fitbit Air with Health Guardian for users with Google Health Premium. This uses data gathered throughout the month from many of the sensors already in the Fitbit — optical heart rate, blood oxygen, skin temperature, and an accelerometer — and warns you of any detected trends that may present potential risks. Until now, only the Google Pixel Watch 5 had this feature, and now the Fitbit Air is also set to receive it. However, note that this feature only provides trend data and cannot provide on-demand insulin or blood glucose levels.
Beyond the newly added health metrics coming with Health Guardian, Google has also greatly improved certain existing features. If you've ever forgotten to start tracking a workout on your Pixel Watch or Fitbit Air, you might've noticed that it often intelligently does so without any manual input. The feature responsible for this is automatic activity detection, which is getting a huge upgrade in October.
Google states that automatic activity detection is going to be twice as accurate. This is possible using an AI model that will analyze context, such as your daily habits, when and how you work out, and manually added data. The number of supported workouts has also been expanded: the feature could initially detect only 10 activities, a number that has now been increased to over 100. The updated list of workouts includes swimming, strength training, certain racket and team sports, and more.
The Fitbit Air is a capable fitness band, but a standalone wrist-based tracker can only do so much by itself. You'll ultimately have to rely on other apps and equipment for specialized measurements, and managing different sources of data can be annoying. Fortunately, Google partners with several third-party health platforms and gives users the ability to sync and import data from a variety of apps and devices.
For instance, users with an Abbott Lingo continuous glucose monitor will soon be able to sync data with Google Health on select Google wearables, including the Fitbit Air. MyFitnessPal Premium users will now also be able to share food-specific logs with Google Health, and your Fitbit Air will get the ability to import lab results directly from Function Health later in the year. Starting early next year, users will also be able to sync Flo Health data with their Fitbit Air to receive more personalized advice from the Google Health Coach.

articles.title_orig: Supreme Court rejects alleged 9/11 mastermind’s attempt to revive plea deal
articles.title_zh: Supreme Court rejects alleged 9/11 mastermind’s attempt to revive plea deal
articles.content_orig:
BREAKING: CNN’s Christiane Amanpour to depart network after 43 years
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court on Monday rejected an appeal brought by Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and two other alleged 9/11 plotters seeking to hold the government to a plea deal it later withdrew.
The court action removes one barrier to Mohammed standing trial before a military commission in 2028, where the death penalty is a possible punishment. He has been held at the U.S. base in Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, since 2006.
Mohammed is accused of being the ringleader of the plot to crash hijacked planes into the World Trade Center in New York and the Pentagon on Sept. 11, 2001. A fourth plane crashed in a field in Pennsylvania.
The other two men who appealed to the Supreme Court were Mustafa Ahmed al-Hawsawi and Walid bin Attash, who are also held at Guantanamo and set to face trial.
The three men had agreed to a plea deal with military prosecutors in 2024, signed off on by a military commission judge, that would have given them life sentences.
But days later, then-Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin rejected the proposal, saying he had the authority to override the deal.
Military courts said he had no such authority but, in an August ruling, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit ruled in favor of the government , prompting the men to appeal to the Supreme Court.
They argued, among other things, that the appeals court had no authority to intervene in the case.
The long delay in Mohammed facing trial was caused partly by concerns about evidence obtained via CIA torture.
A fourth alleged plotter earmarked for trial, Ali Abdul Aziz Ali, was not involved in the appeal.
Lawrence Hurley is a senior Supreme Court reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: Houthi rebels strike a government military camp in southern Yemen, killing at least 53 fighters
articles.title_zh: Houthi rebels strike a government military camp in southern Yemen, killing at least 53 fighters
articles.content_orig:
A Houthi missile attack on the al-AIam military camp in southern Yemen has killed at least 50 people, according to local authorities.
The Houthis launched three ballistic missiles on Monday at the camp in Shabwa governorate during a training exercise, a spokesperson for the Yemeni government forces said.
Officials for the internationally-recognised government and medical sources initially said at least 18 people were killed and more than 30 wounded when the strike hit the facility, at which new security recruits were undergoing training.
However, the numbers have now risen dramatically. The local authority in Shabwa said later on Monday that 53 people had been killed and 200 injured, news agencies reported.
The attack was carried out as fighting continued to rage across Yemen. The civil war with between the Saudi-backed government and rebel Houthis was frozen for some years before the United States and Israel’s war on Iran provoked a return to conflict.
The hostilities escalated rapidly when the Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), seized strategic territory from forces loyal to the government along the Red Sea coast last month.
Government forces, backed by Saudi Arabia, responded with a counteroffensive and then launched the “Dawn of Yemen” operation, which aims to recapture Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa, which the Iran-aligned group seized in 2014.
The Houthis, meanwhile, have stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia, including on Riyadh’s international airport and the state oil company Aramco.
On Monday, Saudi authorities sent alerts to residents of the capital Riyadh warning of “a hostile aerial threat”.
Rashad al-Alimi, the head of the Yemeni Presidential Leadership Council, said those killed in Shabwa were new recruits and promised a “firm response”.
“Targeting recruits reflects the Houthi militia’s approach of resorting to terrorist attacks when under pressure,” he said.
Reporting from Sanaa, Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry said the Houthis claimed responsibility for the attack.
“The Houthis said the attack targeted what they called a ‘Saudi-backed’ military base, referring to Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces who are stationed at military camps across the country,” he said.
“The Houthis say they will continue to target those bases. Spokesperson Yahya Saree says anywhere with a Saudi-backed military presence will be considered a legitimate target.”
Earlier, Yemeni government forces said they targeted Houthi gatherings, vehicles and weapons in al-Aqroudh, al-Shaqab and al-Sarari, south of Taiz, which is suffering from fuel shortages and soaring prices.

articles.title_orig: ‘Happy Birthday, Vlad. Yours, Always.’ - DJT.
articles.title_zh: ‘Happy Birthday, Vlad. Yours, Always.’ - DJT.
articles.content_orig:
In Donald Trump’s telling, he wins everywhere, from Florida to California, when the votes are counted properly, and his campaign rallies do nothing but juice the Republicans he deigns to share the stage with. “MY RALLIES ARE SAVING THE REPUBLICAN PARTY, AGAIN!!!” he wrote this month.
But Punchbowl News notes this morning that Trump’s actions tell a different story. Even though Trump said in September that he’d spend the last month before the midterms rallying the faithful in battleground districts, Trump has been steering well clear of competitive House races, preferring to play defense in parts of the country where voters are friendlier (and his crowds are larger).
This is worth remembering, ahead of whatever stolen-election nonsense Trump tries to pull next month: Deep down, even Trump knows he’s not as popular as he pretends to be. Happy Monday .
Join Will Sommer and Sam Stein today for MAGA Mondays at the early time of 9:00 a.m. EDT on Substack and YouTube .
Almost two weeks ago, on October 7, Donald Trump mentioned offhand that it was Vladimir Putin’s birthday and the two of them had a call set up. The call went ahead two days later, and Trump has been snuggling closer to Russia and taking a sledgehammer to Ukraine ever since.
You could tell the birthday chat was trouble from the jump. Russian media cheerfully reported on the “substance” and “warmth” of the phone call, with Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov reporting that “nobody wanted to hang up first.” The same day, Trump abruptly announced a dramatic swerve in his own energy policy: Far from increasing sanctions pressure on Russia, Trump now said the United States would waive sanctions in order to start buying diesel fuel from Russia directly.
One day later, on Saturday, October 10, Trump still had Putin’s assessment of Ukraine and Volodymyr Zelensky top of mind. “[Zelensky] wants to make problems for the world. He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel,” Trump told reporters . He even called for Zelensky to be removed from office: “I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal, because he could have made many deals, and for some reason never does.” (Maybe it has something to do with Russia demanding he give it huge chunks of Ukraine as the price of peace. Hard to say, really.) The same day, Trump officials threatened that America might stop sharing intelligence with Ukraine if attacks on Russian energy infrastructure continued.
The next day, Trump placed Zelensky in an even greater bind by unilaterally announcing an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine. Neither side had agreed to any such thing. (“They agreed,” Trump added the next day , “because I said they agreed.”) Thanks to Trump’s renewed enthusiasm for Putin’s lies about the war, this announcement created immediate and massive diplomatic asymmetries. Ukraine, desperate to get back in Trump’s good books, immediately began trying to honor the energy ceasefire; Russia, eager to capitalize, kept right on pounding Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
Zelensky’s unilateral honoring of the energy ceasefire did little to change Trump’s mood. Instead, the United States spent last week handicapping Ukraine’s war efforts in big and small ways. On Tuesday, October 13, Russian missiles pounded Kyiv without the usual advance warning provided by U.S. intelligence. That same night, Ukraine discovered that new restrictions had been placed on its Starlink satellite internet service—crucial infrastructure without which it could not pilot its drones. This service would later be partially, but not entirely, restored; subsequent reporting from Reuters said that the order to slow Ukraine’s satellite internet came directly from the White House, although Trump denied that he ordered it personally. (Subsequent reporting suggested Starlink owner Elon Musk was the one who first proposed the slowdown.)
On Friday, October 16, Trump gave Russia even more sanctions relief—preventing new sanctions on Russia and tariffs on buyers of Russian oil from going into effect, although he himself signed those sanctions into law just last month.
Over and over again since the birthday call, Trump has made his new position on the war clear: Nothing but incentives and wheedling praise for Russia, the war’s imperial aggressor, and nothing but threats and insults for Ukraine, the war’s blameless defender. And yesterday, he gave us his clearest explanation of his thinking yet.
“My decision on Russia is a very simple one,” Trump posted on Truth Social.
Why the kid gloves for Russia?
“I . . . don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table,” Trump said. After all, look how nicely Russia was behaving!
“Russia is doing very little, if anything, to help the Islamic Republic of Iran, compared to what they could be doing, and I want to keep it that way, and will, unless stupid people get in the way.”
And anyway, what was so great about Zelensky and Ukraine?
“[Zelensky] is using Diesel Refineries in Russia as a target, knowing that these attacks are seriously hurting the world diesel markets, including in the United States,” Trump went on. “Farmers, ranchers, and businesses of all kinds are suffering greatly from this, but Russia is, nevertheless, sending, at a low price, millions of barrels of diesel to the World.” Zelensky, Trump added, “doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did. He could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now.”
It’s amazing how many of Trump’s psychological pathologies are here on display at once. There is, of course, his bewildering personal adulation of Putin himself, which makes it all too easy for the Russian dictator to feed him out-and-out lies about the state of the conflict and who is responsible. There’s his alpha-dog approach to geopolitics, which he believes shows great strength and in reality shows great weakness: The United States, Trump apparently believes, ought not lift a finger or offer a word of protest if the world’s other great powers decide to invade their neighbors. Instead, those great powers must be cherished and coddled, lest we “drive them away from the bargaining table” and they decide to intervene in our own imperial adventures.
Note how different this argument is from the old MAGA ones about how the whole conflict is an expensive boondoggle halfway around the world that we shouldn’t be involved with at all. Trump, fully in his own imperial era, has jettisoned such provincial “Donroe Doctrine” thinking. He just argues, openly and explicitly, that it’s better for the United States to be allied with Russia. All this is music to Putin’s ears: The Russian dictator, the Wall Street Journal reports , is now proposing a tripartite summit between the United States, Russia, and China to hash out the ultimate fate of Ukraine.
If you’re as sick as we are of our president sucking up to tyrants, ride with us.
There’s another psychological need on display here, too. Over the last month, Trump has deliberately been trying to shift Americans’ focus away from his interminable boondoggle in Iran and back toward the conflict in Ukraine.
Part of the idea is to get them to blame high gas prices not on Trump, who attacked Iran, but on Zelensky and/or Putin. But it’s also a matter of presidential posture. In Iran, Trump looks feckless and weak. He doesn’t have the stomach to escalate the war further, and Iran keeps flatly ignoring his threats to do so: Remember his July ultimatum that he would blow up “ONE BRIDGE OR POWER PLANT” for every ship Iran attacked in the Strait of Hormuz?
In the Russia–Ukraine conflict, however, Trump thinks he looks strong. After all, Ukraine needs the United States—and how better to demonstrate that need than by withholding the things they need while lecturing them that it’s really their own fault? When the focus is on Iran, Trump looks like a wimp. When it’s on Ukraine, he thinks he looks cruel, but also strong. He knows which focus

articles.title_orig: Ukraine claims world’s first drone evacuation of wounded soldier
articles.title_zh: Ukraine claims world’s first drone evacuation of wounded soldier
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine has shared a video showing what it says is the world’s first evacuation of an injured soldier from the frontlines by drone.
The “historic” mission comes just as Kyiv faces a dire turn in its relationship with Washington over the withdrawal of support in its fight against Russia .
Shared by the 92nd Separate Assault Brigade on Monday, the video shows the soldier strapping himself into a large drone and being flown at what appears to be relatively low altitude over blurred-out territory. The drone carefully lowers him down and the drone operator greets him with “Welcome back to the ground!” The video also showed blurred faces of drone operators who carried out the mission.
The post said the unidentified infantryman was wounded while at his position. “Due to intense enemy drone activity and the presence of landmines, evacuation using conventional unmanned ground vehicles was impossible,” the brigade said.
“At that point, the specialists in our unit took it upon themselves to attempt something that had never been done before: evacuating a serviceman using an aerial drone,” it added.
The craft used was a heavy-lift hexacopter, it said, originally designed as a bomber by a Ukrainian manufacturer. It looks about twice the size of the soldier in the video.
The specialists working on the mission had to ensure the drone could carry a human being without flipping over or swaying excessively, according to the unit.
The rescued soldier is currently undergoing treatment and rehabilitation, the brigade added. The squad leader and programmer with the brigade, only identified by his call sign Napalm, called the soldier a “hero” for agreeing to the mission, “having seen and heard the kind of machine that had arrived to get him.”
In a separate statement, Ukraine’s Ground Forces said its drone units are already conducting operations “that were recently considered science fiction.”
The war has increasingly become a technological arms race, with both Ukraine and Russia relying on drones to reduce human casualties.
The conflict has taken a severe toll on both armies, although neither side reports up-to-date numbers of those killed, injured or missing. Ukraine in particular has faced a severe shortage of manpower as it has tried to ramp up recruitment.
Ukraine had a major leap in drone technology this year, allowing it to limit Russian logistics in occupied territories as well as strike deeper inside Russia to target Russian oil refineries , commercial warehouses and data centers .
“This mission proves once again that Ukrainian service members, working in tandem with Ukrainian manufacturers, are setting global trends in the conduct of warfare,” the brigade’s statement added.
Despite hoping that its drone innovation would give it the upper hand at the negotiating table, Kyiv has faced pressure from the U.S. to halt its strikes on Russian oil sites after President Donald Trump signed a diesel deal with the Kremlin earlier this month.
Kyiv has since also reported gaps in intelligence sharing and restrictions on Elon Musk’s Starlink service that is crucial for its drone missions, battlefield communications and air defense.
The drone evacuation comes just days after Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi announced the Ukrainian government had approved an “experimental project” to use drones for medical logistics. Koretskyi said flights would require coordination with the military, and drones would be given a special status and would be identifiable in the air.
“During the war, moving medical cargo by road can cost critical time, especially for transplants,” he said. “Drones will be able to carry medicines, medical products, blood samples, and donor organs between hospitals, including from remote areas.”
Yuliya Talmazan is a reporter for NBC News Digital, based in London.

articles.title_zh: Uber wins bid to throw out £200m black cab claims
articles.content_orig:
Uber has won its bid to throw out claims worth about £340m brought by thousands of London black cab drivers and two former private hire firms.
The claimants alleged the ride-hailing company gave Transport for London (TfL) misleading information when it first got a licence to operate in the capital in 2012.
But a High Court judge ruled the cases had been brought too late and dismissed them without considering whether the allegations were true.
Uber, which denied the claims, said it was pleased the court had thrown them out at the earliest opportunity.
About 13,000 drivers were seeking nearly £200m in damages, Reuters reported, while a claim on behalf of Kabbie and Iride, two private hire firms that have since closed, sought about £140m.
The lawsuits were filed in 2024, and Uber argued they fell outside the six-year limit for bringing such claims.
In a written ruling, Mr Justice Birt said the claimants could have discovered the alleged deception before 2018.
RGL Management, which ran the cases for the claimants, said it was very disappointed and was considering its options with the legal team.
Since gaining its licence, Uber has taken much of the trade once dominated by black cabs.
The company faces a separate case next week, when it challenges HM Revenue and Customs in a tax dispute worth more than £1bn.

articles.content_orig:
A priest has been killed by a falling crucifix at a church in Ecuador as he performed a mass that was being live streamed online.
Patricio Alfredo Sánchez Molinari died on Saturday at the Perpetuo Socorro church in the city of Guayaquil, southern Ecuador, according to a statement from the city’s archdiocese, published on Facebook on Monday.
Video of the incident shows Sánchez leading the mass when a large wooden cross that was standing on the altar behind him falls over and hits him on the head.
Shouting can be heard from the congregation, and several people enter the frame and rush toward the priest.
On Sunday, the church held a eucharist in memory of Sánchez, led by Cardinal Luis Cabrera, archbishop of Guayaquil.
“We are grateful for all of the condolences from around the world, and especially for your prayers for the eternal rest of the soul of Patricio Sánchez,” the statement reads.
According to CNN affiliate Ecuavisa, the priest was preparing to lead a wedding ceremony when the tragedy occurred.
Police have not commented on the incident so far, Ecuavisa reported.
CNN has reached out to the Archdiocese of Guayaquil for comment.

articles.title_orig: Vibe coding is turning the music gear world upside down
articles.title_zh: Vibe coding is turning the music gear world upside down
articles.content_orig:
LLMs have led to an explosion of custom firmware and hacks for synths, samplers, and grooveboxes.
If you spend any time on r/synthesizers or watch a lot of synth videos on YouTube, you’ve probably noticed the explosion of custom firmware for hardware synthesizers, samplers, and grooveboxes . What unites almost all of them is that they were made possible by increasingly sophisticated vibe coding tools.
These sorts of custom firmware were exceedingly rare in the pre-LLM days, and required both deep expertise and an incredible investment of time. It could take weeks or months to add a simple feature like velocity sensitivity to a Korg Volca . Now, hobbyist hackers are able to turn Temu synths into full-fledged grooveboxes in a matter of days.
Elektron’s budget-friendly Model:Cycles , Digitone, Octatrack, and Digitakt have all gained new capabilities with Claude’s help. Roland’s SP-404 MKII , Ableton’s Push 3 and Move , Akai’s MPC Live and MPC One, as well as the vintage MPC 2000, Novation’s Circuit, Arturia’s MicroFreak , and even Zoom’s 14-year-old Multistomp pedal line have all seen new custom firmware released in the last month or so.
Leading the charge is a tiny $70 Yamaha DX-7 clone: the M-Vave FM-1 . It was already on its way to being the synth of the summer. The dirt-cheap price and faithful recreation of classic FM tones made it incredibly popular with first-time synth buyers, hobbyists, and synthfluencers alike. Inevitably, someone wondered how far they could push the hardware and, with the help of AI, kickstarted an arms race.
The FM-1 now has dozens of custom firmwares available. Many of the most popular — Felucca , Sloop , and x0x — list Claude as a contributor on their GitHub page or include explicit disclosures about their use of AI. Baudgirl is also suspected to have been created with the assistance of AI, but the developer did not reply to a request for comment.
What started as a surprisingly good, but basic DX-7 clone now supports a variety of synth engines, including virtual analog, sample playback, multi-track sequencing, and a variety of UI designs.
It’s not terribly shocking that someone was willing to risk bricking a $70 Temu synth. Generally, the gear that has benefited from this surge of vibe-coded custom firmware is older or more affordable.
Roman Rusinov, who posts on Reddit as themanro and releases music under Farlow, set his sights on the Zoom MS-70CDR. It’s a budget multi-effects pedal from 2012 that has a reputation for punching above its weight, making it a staple of affordable synth setups. He started by learning about ZDL , a project that reverse-engineered the Multistomp format, allowing for the creation of custom effects. He eventually coaxed the pedal into running NAM A2 Lite captures and custom impulse responses (IRs), turning it into a full-fledged modeler capable of emulating vintage amps.
“I was already using AI for some work stuff and figured this would be a great case to try learning some vibe-coding fundamentals and get a project going,” he told The Verge . “There was a lot of trial and error of finding the limitations of the hardware and software.” He says he’s thrilled to be part of a broader movement. “Somehow it all lined up with all these other projects pushing the boundaries of older hardware and breathing new life into it. I love that,” he said. “If you own the hardware, you should be able to do whatever you want with it.”
18nelli, the developer behind Modded Cycles , was similarly motivated by a desire to revitalize some forgotten gear. “I had an Elektron Model:Cycles that left me feeling frustrated,” he told The Verge . He said that it felt designed “just to push us to buy their more expensive gear.” But recent AI advances made him believe he could add features to the groovebox, which hasn’t had an official update since May 2021.
So he opened up his Cycles, documented all the parts, and started working with Claude Code to implement his first hack — six-track audio over USB. That has since exploded into a community project with multiple mods contributed by others, several standalone custom firmwares , and even the ability to turn your Model:Cycles into a Model:Samples. “I think not using LLMs would have been counterproductive,” he said. “I probably would have spent a massive amount of time and energy on just a single feature, whereas my real goal is to actually create and make music with amazing mods.”
Modded Cycles has certainly been one of the more frantic projects out there. I recently watched as five firmware updates hit the announcements channel on its Discord in one day. 18nelli has since said he plans to pause adding new features and slow development to polish the existing code and stomp out some bugs.
New mods and firmwares hit the web almost every day now. If there’s a favorite piece of gear in your arsenal that you wish had one killer feature, there’s a chance it might end up on a GitHub page sooner than later. Heck, if you just wish your pocket synth could play NES ROMs , that’s also a distinct possibility.
Of course, there is some risk here. These firmwares are often less thoroughly tested than the manufacturer’s official one. The response to the modding scene has varied from company to company, with many choosing to remain silent. Elektron banned links to custom firmware from their forums. In a statement posted on its official forums, the company said, “We would always warn against modifications to our firmware and/or machines that could brick them … Something that looks like a simple change in isolation can lead to major problems elsewhere, particularly when a later official OS arrives, and can confuse users about which features are officially available on our machines.”
Others, like M-Vave, seem to be embracing the movement. It recently announced FM1 Open , an open-source firmware with additional features, plus a development kit and a firmware-flashing tool for the community.
The response to music gear that uses AI and vibe coding has been mixed. Devices like the Polyend Endless have sparked some ire . And music-making subreddits are awash in people complaining about vibe-coded plugin slop . But so far the community has been less hostile to vibe-coded firmware. Maybe, in part, because breathing new life into old instruments helps keep their Gear Acquisition Syndrome (GAS) in check.

articles.title_orig: Elon Musk says he's giving SpaceX stock to every kid in America
articles.title_zh: Elon Musk says he's giving SpaceX stock to every kid in America
articles.content_orig:
Elon Musk has said he will give every child in America a stake in SpaceX, his $2 trillion aerospace and artificial intelligence company, as tech firms face intensifying scrutiny over their impact on society.
“Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America,” he wrote on X on Monday. “This will be the first of many.”
SpaceX only began trading publicly in June (and after the biggest initial public offering in history ). The company’s shares were trading for about $146 when the market closed on Friday.
Musk’s proposal was thin on detail. It is not clear how those shares would be distributed to the tens of millions of American children or whether all of them would even be eligible.
According to the United States Census Bureau, there are roughly 73 million people under the age of 18, making Musk’s potential giveaway worth about $10.7 billion at SpaceX’s current share price.
Offering young people a stake in the US stock market isn’t a new idea. This month, the Treasury Department automatically signed up millions of under-18s to Trump Accounts, a new federal savings and investment vehicle, with children born between the start of 2025 and the end of 2028 eligible for a one-off $1,000 government contribution.
In July, SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell and her husband pledged to donate one SpaceX share to each of roughly 2 million children already signed up to an account. The couple said they will prioritize donations to children from lower-income households and in SpaceX’s home state of Texas.
How two billionaires are shaping America’s return to the moon
Musk’s offer came in response to Anthropic’s announcement on Sunday that it will commit at least 5% of its shares — worth $48 billion at the private company’s latest valuation — to a “Public Benefit Fund” that will donate money to social causes.
The fund could make “large donations” to nonprofit organizations or “direct distributions to specific populations,” the company wrote on its website, adding that the money could help mitigate the impact of artificial intelligence on people’s jobs.
Musk, the world’s richest person, retorted on X : “I recommend giving the shares directly to the public… This is what I will be doing.”
Musk signed the Giving Pledge in 2012 — a commitment by the world’s richest people to donate the majority of their wealth to charitable causes during their lifetime or in their wills.
His charitable organization, the Musk Foundation, focuses on grant-giving in a handful of fields including renewable energy, space exploration and pediatric research, according to its website .
According to a New York Times analysis last year, the foundation held more than $14 billion in assets at the end of 2024, making it one of the largest in the United States. But the Times said the foundation’s donations that year went largely to organizations closely connected to Musk’s business interests.
SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Times’ claims.
‘Musk’ documentary examines the world’s richest man
Musk has also openly questioned the effectiveness of traditional charitable giving. Speaking about philanthropy on the People by WTF podcast last year, Musk said: “We should try to do things that help our fellow human beings.”
“The biggest challenge I find with my foundation is trying to give money away in a way that is truly beneficial to people,” he said. “It’s very easy to give money away to get the appearance of goodness. It is very difficult to give money away for the reality of goodness.”
In 2021, Musk said he would sell $6 billion-worth of Tesla stock and donate it to the United Nations’ World Food Programme if the organization could demonstrate how the money would “solve world hunger.” It does not appear that Musk has yet donated the sum.
Both Musk’s and Anthropic’s offers come as AI companies face intense backlash over the safety of their products (Anthropic itself recently warned of the “existential risk to humanity” posed by the technology), the potential for AI to push humans out of their jobs en masse, as well as the social and environmental impact of the industry’s gargantuan data center buildout.
Tech titans more broadly are catching heat.
New movies like “The Social Reckoning” — about a Facebook employee blowing the whistle on unsafe company practices — and documentary “You Can See Everything” — following blood testing start-up founder and convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes — are helping to remind audiences of the long-running recklessness of some in Big Tech.
Musk himself is the subject of the new documentary “Musk,” charting his life and career. It is unsparing in its criticism of some of his business practices and his controversial foray into politics.

articles.title_orig: Toulouse to Ho Chi Minh City: Five fast-rising cities that should be on travellers' radars right now
articles.title_zh: Toulouse to Ho Chi Minh City: Five fast-rising cities that should be on travellers' radars right now
articles.content_orig:
A new global report spotlights the world's emerging urban hotspots. From thriving cultural scenes to changing neighbourhoods, locals reveal what makes them worth exploring now.
New York, London and Paris have once again topped Oxford Economics' annual ranking of the world's leading cities . But beyond these familiar names, its 2026 Global Cities Index has identified 28 " cities to watch " – places whose rapid growth and rising fortunes could see them become increasingly influential in the years ahead.
These cities aren't just growing economically. New neighbourhoods, thriving cultural scenes and improved transport links are already reshaping the visitor experience and making them increasingly interesting places to visit.
We selected five from the list and spoke to people who know them well to find out what's changing – and why they're worth exploring now.
With its population forecast to grow by 57,000 over the next four years – more than anywhere else in France – Toulouse is one of Europe's fastest-growing cities and is attracting younger, skilled newcomers with its mild climate, relatively affordable cost of living and high quality of life.
"Here, you don't have to choose between slow life and fast life," said Elodie Paramelle, who recently returned to Toulouse after 10 years in London. "You get the energy of a big city, with an incredible food scene, independent cafes, cocktail bars and a growing cultural offering, alongside a much slower pace of life."
Toulouse has changed significantly in recent years, according to Mélodie Tyler, who moved back here after seven years in Paris. She says the city is much more walkable and bike-friendly, while its food and wine scene has expanded dramatically. And she notes that the buzz is spreading beyond the historic centre. "Ponts-Jumeaux where I live hosts a bunch of festivals, guinguettes [open-air bars] and skateboarding competitions," she said. "The Toulousains love to party and be outside as much as possible!"
Beyond its thriving neighbourhoods, Toulouse is also major aerospace hub, home to hundreds of companies, including Airbus's global headquarters. Visitors can explore that heritage at the Cité de l'Espace space-themed discovery centre or Aeroscopia aviation museum beside the Airbus runways. For something more unusual, La Halle de La Machine brings art and engineering together through giant mechanical creatures created by a local street theatre company.
Vietnam's largest city is on a remarkable trajectory. Oxford Economics predicts Ho Chi Minh City will be among the world's 50 fastest-growing cities over the next five years, with an economy that could rival Berlin's by 2050. Tourism is booming too, with more than eight million international visitors last year, exceeding projections.
"The first metro line only opened at the end of 2024, and it's one of the most tangible symbols of how quickly the city is changing," said Meaghan Yash, a travel specialist at tour operator Timbuktu Travel who frequently designs trips here. The 20km (12.5 mile) line runs from Ben Thanh Market in the city centre to the Suoi Tien theme park, with single fares costing less than £1 ($1.33).
Yet, Ho Chi Minh's appeal lies in how it balances change with continuity. Chris Buchart, commercial director at Vietnamese hotel company Fusion Group, suggests travellers visit the French-colonial Central Post Office and Opera House , and then the War Remnants Museum for context on the country's history, before turning to one of the city's greatest strengths: its food.
Buchart recommends trying bánh mì (Vietnamese baguette sandwich) , cơm tấm (broken rice) and bánh xèo (crispy pancakes), while Yash suggests venturing beyond the usual tourist circuit in central District 1 to quieter, more residential neighbourhoods where leafy streets are ideal for wandering and cafe-hopping. He also suggests Chợ Lớn, the city's historic Chinatown, for its markets, temples and medicine shops, while across the river in Thảo Điền, independent boutiques, galleries and home-grown Vietnamese brands make for excellent shopping.
The Polish capital has made one of the fastest jumps in the Global Cities index, climbing more than 100 places to 61st. Its quality-of-life score now surpasses London, New York and Tokyo, while its economy is projected to expand by around 3% annually – nearly twice the European city average.
For Konrad Warzecha, a Polish-Australian whose family home is in Warsaw's Wola district, the transformation has been remarkable. "From our balcony you can see the skyline, and watching the roads, highways and towers go up over 20 years has made the city almost unrecognisable," said Warzecha, who blogs at House Sitters Guide .
The biggest changes, he says, are on the streets. "As a kid I rode the trams and did not feel safe, and I saw many robberies happen," he said. "Now I have never felt safer. People walk around at night, the streets are clean and trouble gets dealt with quickly."
For first-time visitors, Warzecha recommends a walk that takes in both the old and new city. He starts at the Soviet-era Palace of Culture and Science and follows Nowy Świat boulevard into the Old Town , painstakingly rebuilt after World War Two.
Along the way, he stops for pączki (Polish doughnuts) and a meal at a bar mleczny, one of the city's traditional, no-frills milk bars. "It tastes like home cooking," he said. "A three-course meal with drinks comes to around £13 ($17).
Warzecha once wanted to leave Poland and move back to Australia, but today his feelings have changed. "These days Warsaw is one of the places I recommend most, and not because I am from there. I am proud to have a Polish background."
Medellín's remarkable transformation is reflected in its economic fortunes. Employment in business and financial services has more than doubled over the past 20 years, and Oxford Economics predicts that the Colombian city's average income will overtake Buenos Aires and São Paulo by the 2040s.
"In the 10 years I've lived here, Medellín has gone from a curiosity for only the most daring to a hub for travel," said Patrick Quinn, who runs the Colombia Writers Retreat in nearby El Peñol. "Once blighted or overlooked places like Comuna 13, Perpetuo Socorro and Ciudad del Río have become cultural and economic centres."
The city's Metrocable , the first urban cable car system designed for mass public transport, carries commuters and visitors up the surrounding hillsides, while emerging creative districts are giving travellers new reasons to explore. "There is enough happening in its food, art and design scenes to warrant several days in its own right," said Joanna Rigby Jones, a travel specialist at Timbuktu Travel who has planned trips here for years. She recommends the creative district, Perpetuo Socorro , for design shops, galleries and speciality coffee.

Comuna 13 , once one of the city's most dangerous districts, now draws some of Medellín's biggest crowds. "Go with a local guide who can provide the context behind the murals, escalators and music rather than treating the neighbourhood simply as an Instagram backdrop," said Rigby Jones.
Quinn also recommends exploring the Poblado and Laureles neighbourhoods, seeking out local creators and curators. "That way, you can go home and tell stories that will dismantle outdated misconceptions about this place," he said.
Once heavily dependent on oil, Abu Dhabi has transformed its economy through investment in technology, renewable energy, property and finance. The UAE capital now ranks sixth in the Global Cities index for the skills and education of its workforce, ahead of Paris and Boston, while its non-oil economy and job market are projected to surpass neighbouring Dubai.
