articles.title_orig: Strait of Hormuz crisis traps 6,000 sailors as attacks on ships mount, UN maritime chief says
articles.title_zh: Strait of Hormuz crisis traps 6,000 sailors as attacks on ships mount, UN maritime chief says
articles.content_orig:
International Maritime Organization Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez discusses efforts to communicate with Tehran as attacks escalate and commercial shipping faces growing risks.
Thousands of sailors remain stranded near the Strait of Hormuz amid escalating attacks on commercial ships, the United Nations' top maritime official warned Sunday after Iran accused the U.S. military of using an international emergency radio channel to threaten civilian crews.
The warning also came amid reports that 24 ships had been attacked on the waterway over roughly two weeks, underscoring growing concerns about maritime safety in the region, according to Financial Times .
"The situation continues to be severe and critical when it comes to international shipping," International Maritime Organization (IMO) Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez told Fox News Digital.
"There is a double blockade and too many vessels have been attacked, particularly in recent days.
'VAST MAJORITY' OF IRAN'S ATTEMPTED ATTACKS ON STRAIT OF HORMUZ ARE UNSUCCESSFUL, CENTCOM SPOKESMAN SAYS
24 ships have been attacked on the waterway over roughly two weeks, according to reports. (Fatemeh Bahrami / Anadolu via Getty Images)
"Seafarers have continued to perish in these attacks and around 6,000 seafarers remain trapped since the beginning of the conflict," he warned, adding that his message was not to transit the Strait of Hormuz or put seafarers at risk "until we have guarantees."
Dominguez's warning followed an Oct. 9 letter to the IMO in which Iran alleged that the U.S. military used VHF Channel 16 , an internationally designated maritime distress and safety channel, to intimidate Iranian crews in the Persian Gulf.
"VHF Channel 16 has been repeatedly occupied for prolonged periods by the United States military forces operating in the Persian Gulf," the letter stated.
TRUMP OPENS HORMUZ UNDER FIRE WITH ‘PROJECT FREEDOM’ AS IRAN WARNS OF ATTACKS
Smoke column rises from tanker El Gaia after incident in the Strait of Hormuz.
"During such transmissions, Iranian seafarers have been addressed in Persian with threatening, abusive and provocative language and in certain instances urged to abandon their vessels."
In a statement to Fox News Digital, U.S. Central Command defended its enforcement of the naval blockade of Iranian ports .
"The U.S. naval blockade has been in place for months and is professionally communicated to all international mariners," CENTCOM said.
"Vessels that refuse to comply with blockade enforcement receive multiple warnings, with ample opportunity to comply.
"American forces remain highly vigilant, focused, and professional while fully enforcing the naval blockade against Iran ."
Iran's complaint was submitted by Seyed Ali Mousavi, its ambassador to the IMO, and circulated to member states on Oct. 9, according to a copy reviewed by Fox News Digital.
Tehran also accused American forces of turning the maritime safety channel into an "instrument of military intimidation and psychological pressure against civilian crews."
The letter cited commercial vessels, shipping companies and maritime operators but provided no recordings, transcripts or specific details of the alleged exchanges. Fox News Digital could not independently verify the accusations.
IRAN THREATENS TO HALT RED SEA TRAFFIC IN RESPONSE TO US MILITARY BLOCKADE OF PORTS
Naval units from Iran simulate the rescue of a hijacked vessel during joint drills at the Port of Bandar Abbas in Hormozgan, Iran, on Feb. 19, 2026. (Iranian Army/Handout/Anadolu via Getty Images)
"Seafarers are not trained for combat, and they are not guilty of any conflicts that are happening around the world," Dominguez said.
"And we have seen this in several parts of the world where Channel 16, that should not be used for this kind of communication, starts receiving messages that may be perceived as actually threatening or that are outside the remit of why it was created."
Iran also asked the IMO to raise its allegations with member states and relevant international organizations, potentially including the International Telecommunication Union.
Dominguez said the IMO could review its regulations and procedures to determine whether stronger safeguards are needed, though he did not announce a formal investigation.
"Our role here at IMO is that when those situations take place, we will then look into any technical measures or any operational aspects that we may need to clarify further within our regulatory framework," he said, stressing that member states have equal rights to raise concerns, regardless of the conflict.
"We have a responsibility, and I have a duty as well, to circulate letters and notes that the countries actually put forward when they're also being affected."
WHO CONTROLS THE STRAIT OF HORMUZ RIGHT NOW? HERE'S WHAT THE SHIP TRAFFIC ACTUALLY SHOWS
The U.S. naval blockade has been in place for months and is professionally communicated to all international mariners, CENTCOM said. (U.S. Navy)
"We take all that information, meet at the level of different meetings of the organization and have the discussions," Dominguez added.
"If it's demonstrated that we probably need to improve our rules in order to avoid communications issues, or that we need to enhance the knowledge of how these channels should be used, that is a role for us."
The IMO had recorded 100 confirmed maritime incidents across the region as of Oct. 9, with 24 seafarers killed since the conflict began Feb. 28. Dominguez also warned that fraudulent ship registrations and false flags have become major contributors to the danger.
"What we've also seen right now is an increase in fraudulent registries with false flags that are taking the risk and acting as shuttle tankers in order to bring goods in and out," he said. "That's one of the reasons that we're seeing an escalation.
"And it's the irresponsible shipowners that are taking the risk in order to actually be able to trade and move some of the goods and the cargoes."
WHITE HOUSE SILENT ON IRAN-OMAN HORMUZ PLAN TEHRAN SAYS WOULD BAN US WARSHIPS
A ship is seen passing through the Strait of Hormuz during a two-week temporary ceasefire between the United States and Iran on April 8, 2026. (Shady Alassar/Anadolu/Getty Images)
"For me, any single case, any vessel that is attacked, any life of a seafarer that is lost, is a critical situation for me, because they are all relevant, they are all important."
Despite the confrontation, Dominguez said diplomatic channels with Iran remain open, though he has no direct contact with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
"I have communications with all the member states of IMO, and that includes the Islamic Republic of Iran," he said.
"Of course, that's through the diplomatic channels. I don't have direct contact with the IRGC .
"I have conversations with them and they respond to my messages. You know, the information flows. What is difficult is to get final decisions because of the conflict that is ongoing."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Fox News Digital has reached out to the Iranian embassy for comment.
Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

articles.title_orig: Burnham warns of Neets-fuelled 'economic catastrophe and moral failure'
articles.title_zh: Burnham warns of Neets-fuelled 'economic catastrophe and moral failure'
articles.content_orig:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has warned the UK faces an "economic catastrophe and moral failure" due to the nearly one million young people not in education, employment or training.
Writing in the Times newspaper , Burnham has laid out his case for the government to "invest in the success of our young people" rather than "pay for failure through the benefits system".
"Benefits will become the backstop, not the starting point," Burnham wrote in his piece published in Monday's paper.
Later this week, the government is expected to announce plans to give young people thousands of job opportunities. The Conservative Party has labelled the government's youth employment strategy "a disaster".
According to the latest data from the Office for National Statistics, there are almost a million people aged 16 to 24 known as Neets - not in education, employment or training.
In his opinion column, the prime minister said this reflected a "generation being denied its chance to get on in life".
"This is an economic catastrophe and a moral failure. And it must change," he wrote.
Burnham said two years of Covid lockdowns, social media that erodes "confidence and sense of belonging", an education system focused on the "university route", job markets with "too few opportunities" and failures of previous governments have all contributed to the Neets crisis.
"Today, the welfare system provides an assessment, a payment and, after that, goodbye," Burnham wrote. "Too often there is no support, no offer of skills and no opportunity to get a job."
He flagged a shift in the approach to welfare, which he said "will no longer begin by establishing which benefits a young person is entitled to" but rather "begin with their ambitions and the help they need to achieve them".
The prime minister added: "The safety net will always be there for those who cannot work. But if someone can work with the right help, the government has a duty to do everything in its power to make that happen."
Ministers are this week set to release plans for tens of thousands of new youth apprenticeships and placements in the construction industry, and at accounting, consulting and legal firms.
Shadow Business and Trade Secretary Julia Lopez said: "Labour have been a disaster for youth jobs. Their tax hikes and red tape have made it harder for businesses to hire, invest and grow, destroying opportunities for young people looking to take their first step on the career ladder."
Burnham confirmed the long-awaited full review of young people and work will be published next month, and vowed to take its recommendations "seriously".
The review's author, former health secretary Alan Milburn, has argued for the need to "redistribute money from the welfare system to more employment support" in an interview with the Guardian published on Sunday.
"This is not a workshy, snowflake generation," Milburn said. "If we provide more opportunities and we provide more support, the overwhelming majority of young people will take that, because that's what they want. The system isn't delivering what young people want, which is a job."
Milburn calculated that the government spends 25 times more on benefits for young people than getting them into work, describing the current rate of Neets as "shameful" .
Chancellor John Healey, who is due to hand down his first budget on 28 October, told the Labour party conference in September the government had a "moral duty" to address welfare spending.

articles.title_orig: Here’s What a $10,000 Investment in Nvidia Stock Will Be Worth by 2030
articles.title_zh: Here’s What a $10,000 Investment in Nvidia Stock Will Be Worth by 2030
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia ( NVDA -1.43% ) has made investors significantly richer over the past four years, turning a $10,000 investment into nearly $179,000 as of this writing.
This massive surge in Nvidia's shares has been fueled by the advent of artificial intelligence (AI). When OpenAI's ChatGPT , introduced publicly in November 2022, became a big hit, companies lined up to buy Nvidia's graphics processing units (GPUs) after it emerged that the semiconductor giant's chips played an instrumental role in training the chatbot.
The AI economy and Nvidia have come a long way since then. AI is now finding its way into several industries, boosting productivity and economic growth. The good news for Nvidia investors is that AI adoption isn't showing any signs of slowing, which explains why the company continues to deliver robust growth even after becoming significantly larger over the past four years.
We will take a closer look at the company's prospects in this article and assess whether investing $10,000 in Nvidia stock over the next five years could be a profitable move.
Nvidia's AI-driven surge has made it the world's largest company with a market cap of $5.2 trillion. So, expecting another 20x jump in Nvidia's stock price over the next five years would be quite absurd, as it would put its market cap past $100 trillion. However, that doesn't mean Nvidia stock can't climb higher over the next five years.
NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 10/16/26
After all, the company is still growing at an impressive pace despite the scale it has achieved. Nvidia's revenue in the first six months of fiscal 2027 (which will end in January 2027) increased by 96% over the same period last year to $177.8 billion. The company expects fiscal Q3 revenue of $108 billion, an 89% jump from the year-ago period.
Analysts expect a 91% spike in Nvidia's revenue for fiscal 2027 to $411.6 billion. Meanwhile, earnings per share are expected to almost double in fiscal 2027 to $9.31. Importantly, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is confident that the company's growth will continue unabated next year. He recently noted at a conference that the number of chips the company sells will double in 2027, according to CNBC .
Huang added that continued investments in AI infrastructure will drive this incredible growth, as companies and governments look to make the most of the technology's benefits. For example, the World Economic Forum noted earlier this year that AI could increase labor productivity by 1.5% to 3% over the next decade, citing the chief economist of consulting giant EY.
Moreover, investors will do well to note that AI is moving beyond data centers into real-world applications, such as robots and cars. Known as physical AI, Nvidia is pushing into this niche where machines can make complex decisions on their own. From performing precision-related tasks such as threading needles in surgical wards to operating on a conveyor belt, Nvidia is moving into a new frontier that could supercharge its long-term growth.
Nvidia's physical AI offerings are already being used by the likes of Amazon and Japan's national AI venture, and I won't be surprised to see the tech giant pulling in more customers. That's because the physical AI market's revenue is expected to grow to 430 billion euros by 2030, suggesting this niche could move the needle significantly for Nvidia over the next five years.
Throw in the $3 trillion to $4 trillion revenue opportunity that Nvidia sees in the AI infrastructure market in 2030, and it is easy to see why analysts have become extremely bullish about its growth prospects through fiscal 2029 (which will end in January 2029).
NVDA Revenue Estimates for Current Fiscal Year data by YCharts
According to the above chart, Nvidia's revenue could increase by 68% in fiscal 2028, which is almost in line with the company's guidance of 70% growth. That's expected to be followed by a 30% increase in fiscal 2029 to $900 billion. There is a solid chance Nvidia will maintain strong growth in fiscal years 2030 and 2031 as well, which could set the stock up for further gains.
Let's assume Nvidia's top line increases by even 10% in fiscal 2030 and 2031 (which will end in January 2031), its top line could reach $1.09 trillion in 2030 (given that fiscal 2031 will coincide with the majority of calendar 2030).
Now, this AI stock trades at 18 times sales. Assuming Nvidia trades at half of this sales multiple after five years, its market cap could jump to $9.8 trillion (based on the $1.09 trillion revenue estimate). That implies a potential upside of 88% from current levels. So, a $10,000 investment in this semiconductor stock will be worth more than $18,800 by 2030.
However, that could be a conservative estimate, as Nvidia could grow faster and command a premium valuation after five years. That's why investors can still consider buying this AI bellwether, as it has the potential to make investors richer owing to emerging niches within the AI ecosystem.

articles.title_orig: Report: Putin wants to discuss Ukraine's future with Trump and Chinese president - without Zelensky
articles.title_zh: Report: Putin wants to discuss Ukraine's future with Trump and Chinese president - without Zelensky
articles.content_orig:
Russian President Vladimir Putin proposed a meeting with US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping next month to discuss ending the Russia-Ukraine war, the Wall Street Journal reported Sunday night, citing people familiar with the discussions.
The talks would not involve Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky , an unprecedented move which would be expected to alarm many European countries, WSJ wrote.
According to the report, the Kremlin suggested the three leaders meet on the sidelines of the upcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, which takes place Nov. 18 and 19 in Shenzhen, southern China.
Putin first suggested the meeting while speaking to Trump on October 9, in the same conversation in which the two leaders agreed that the US would buy Russian diesel fuel and facilitate its sale, a former Russian intelligence officer told WSJ .
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov confirmed that discussions over a potential meeting were ongoing.
“There is no clear understanding yet regarding the meeting itself or its potential agenda, although all three parties acknowledge the hypothetical possibility of such a meeting taking place,” he told WSJ .
A senior US official told WSJ that Trump hadn't agreed to the meeting but may be receptive to the idea due to his desire to end the war.
This comes as Trump and Zelensky publicly criticize the other's decisions, with Zelensky saying on Saturday that Trump's decision to waive sanctions on Russia and tariffs on its goods days before they were to take effect will embolden Moscow to keep attacking Ukraine, and Trump suggesting that Ukraine needs a new president.
Trump claimed that Zelensky "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did," in a post on Truth Social earlier on Sunday, calling on the Ukrainian leader to stop attacking Russian diesel refineries.
Neither the White House nor the Chinese Embassy in Washington has commented on the report, but analysts told WSJ that a meeting between Trump, Xi, and Putin could advance Xi's ambitions for China's place in global diplomacy.
“China wants to be seen as the pivot of the great powers, and potentially as a mediator between the US and Russia,” Yun Sun, director of the China program at the Stimson Center, a Washington think tank, told WSJ .
However, Chinese officials have expressed concern that the meeting could overshadow China's role in the region at APEC, according to the report.
People familiar with the discussions told WSJ that Xi is also trying to balance support for Putin and economic ties with Europe. A meeting with Putin and Trump to discuss Ukraine could raise the risk of European backlash.
Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: EU tariffs aimed at China hitting Ukraine, steel boss says
articles.title_zh: EU tariffs aimed at China hitting Ukraine, steel boss says
articles.content_orig:
The boss of one of Ukraine's biggest steel companies has called on the European Union to drop import restrictions on products made from the country, arguing it has been "bundled together" in measures aimed a curbing cheap imports from the likes of China.
Yuriy Ryzhenkov, chief executive of Metinvest, told the BBC the recently-imposed tariffs on imported steel to the EU were "unfair" and had been put in place "without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in".
He said he wished to see "at least a carve out" for Ukraine to access the EU market.
A spokesperson for the European Commission said the EU "took into account the difficult situation" of Ukraine when deciding its steel policy.
The trading bloc has recently imposed restrictions on steel imports in an effort to protect steel manufacturers of member nations.
It has capped the amount of steel which can enter the EU tax free at 18.3 million tonnes per year - a 47% reduction from 2024 levels.
There are some country-specific quotas in the policy, but the overall aim is to cut the amount of steel that can be imported due to member nations struggling to compete with cheap imports from the likes of China and Turkey.
Despite a free-trade agreement (FTA) being in place between the EU and Ukraine, the FTA does not stop the EU from introducing separate trade protection measures.
"Ukraine has been bundled together into those measures without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in," Ryzhenkov said, pointing to the war with Russia.
"Access to the European market is crucial for survival," he added. "The restrictive measures that have been put in place by the authorities in the European Union, they don't help.
"I think it's unfair that Ukraine has been treated in the same way as all of the other importers into the European Union."
The Ukraine steel industry estimates steel exports to the EU could ultimately fall by about 50–60%.
The EU said Ukraine's specific steel quota guaranteed exports of the metal, but acknowledged this was at a "level lower than in the past years".
"Despite the war effort, Ukraine remains an important exporter of steel to the EU," a spokesperson said, adding it had "offered compensations" to its largest suppliers, which included Ukraine.
Steel products are a foundation in Ukraine's economy. Before the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, metallurgy and mining accounted for roughly 10% of Ukraine's national income and a third of its exports. The EU is its top customer.
But the industry has suffered from the continued Russian bombardment.
All of Ukraine's steel mills have been bombed at points since the conflict began in 2022, but Ryzhenkov said strikes had "intensified significantly recently".
At one point in September, there was "no single tonne of steel produced" in Ukraine for the first time in about 150 years, he added.
Almost 800 Metinvest workers have been killed since the war began.
Ryzhenkov said the company had "improved the covered areas" at its mills where workers can shelter during air raids.
"The only thing we can do is to design procedures to keep people safe and just obey those procedures and try to minimise the risks."
"Unfortunately, you cannot cover a whole steel mill to avoid it being damaged."
Ryzhenkov said he expected the coming winter to be "one of the hardest in our history".
"We are in a dire situation when we don't have logistics to access any other market apart from the EU and cutting our available market by 60%, that doesn't help for the industry to survive."

articles.title_orig: France in Shock After Protests Turn Into Riots, Damaging Buildings and Shops
articles.title_zh: France in Shock After Protests Turn Into Riots, Damaging Buildings and Shops
articles.content_orig:
France’s President Emmanuel Macron addressed the nation on Sunday evening as communities reeled from one of the most violent nights of unrest in recent years after largely peaceful anti-government protests descended into rioting, leaving government buildings torched, one police officer and one protester dead.
Macron said that the full force of the law would be brought to bear on those who had damaged property or participated in rioting.
“Those who destroyed must pay,” Macron said. “Those who looted must pay back. Those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable.”
Macron described the violence as the work of “seditious elements from far-left factions, joined by numerous delinquents.”
“Watching these images, we were all wondering: what had got into them? How can French people do that to France?”
“Nothing can justify it, explain it or excuse it,” Macron said. “Tonight we all feel both anger and shame.”
The president added that the government should listen to public grievances, and that many protesters did not participate in violence.
“Yesterday, hundreds of thousands of our compatriots demonstrated to state legitimate claims,” Macron said. “Never must we confuse the latter with those who destroyed and vandalized.”
Macron said that he had asked the government to convene stakeholders – including students, teachers, trade unionists and others – this week to discuss “concrete proposals.”
There were at least two deaths connected to rioting and protests over the weekend. A 22-year-old police officer died after being “struck by a third-party vehicle” in the city of Nantes, about 250 miles southwest of Paris, France’s Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said .
One protester died just north of Paris following a “cardiorespiratory arrest,” CNN affiliate BFMTV reported on Sunday , citing the Paris Police headquarters.
Police have detained more than 2,000 people, Nunez said, adding that more than 600 police officers were injured.
Scenes unfolded again on Sunday of police officers launching tear gas into the hallowed Place de la République, where dozens of people gathered in response to messages on social media to “continue the movement,” BFMTV reported. In the central city of Limoges, the 143-year-old town hall was set ablaze on Saturday, with video showing its spire collapsing. In Marseille, masked protesters dressed all in black broke into city hall and defaced the building, and in Lyon, protesters torched the city’s tourist office.
Lawmakers and regional officials launched mounting criticism over the government’s law enforcement plan, BFMTV said, with French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu set to meet the mayors of Paris, Lyon and Marseille, who called for greater reinforcement to repair the damage.
As night fell in Paris on Saturday, groups of young people looted shops and started fires as protests wound down, prompting police to respond with tear gas and baton charges in the narrow streets. Alexandre Bompard, CEO of retail giant Carrefour, said in a social media post Sunday that around 1,500 stores across the country were affected by violence.
More than 600 police officers have been injured, France’s Interior Minister Laurent Nunez posted on X on Sunday, warning that “nothing can justify” the unrest. Earlier this weekend, Lecornu also condemned “unacceptable levels of violence.”
The destruction followed what had been largely peaceful protests, which have grown out of sweeping student-led rallies that gripped parts of France last month, sparking a broader movement against crumbling schools, the spiking cost of living, and perceived government inaction. The rallies have become emblematic of long-simmering, intergenerational anger among people who say their calls for social and political change are going unmet by negligent governments.
Some 550,000 protesters hit the streets across France, including 110,000 in Paris, Nunez said on Saturday. Organizers said far more people turned out.
“There’s an accumulation of wealth and power that’s completely out of control,” one protester, who gave her name as Pauline, told CNN in Paris on Saturday.
“We’re also here to support the youth. There are victories, but if we look at the bigger picture, it’s not going in the right direction,” the 36-year-old added.
Another demonstrator complained of “less democracy” and a “concentration of power” under Macron’s leadership. “There are billionaires who control the media,” Louise, 38, told CNN. “We are fighting to change things.”
Macron slammed “sowers of chaos” for interfering with peaceful protests, and warned late on Saturday that “those who have broken, attacked (police) prefectures, as well as businesses, looted even our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished.”
“We do not back down in the face of rioters and those who’ve come to attack law enforcement,” said the Paris Police Prefecture – the body that oversees the Paris Police Force, emergency services and various other administrative departments – adding that its staffers stood “their ground with courage and professionalism.”
The police response to the weeks of protest has come under scrutiny. Earlier in the week, that response had left a 14-year-old boy with a fractured jaw. Another police officer was captured on camera using a headlock on a girl in the northwestern area of Alençon, an action now prohibited by law.
A protester in the city of Saint-Étienne, about 40 miles southwest of Lyon, lost his hand during a march there on Saturday, a police source told BFMTV.
This is the second reported instance of a demonstrator losing their hand in the current wave of student protests.
A student in the northeastern city of Lens lost his hand after reportedly picking up a grenade earlier this month, prompting the temporary suspension of one type of stun grenade by police. That ban, which still allowed police to use several different grenades, has now been rescinded.
Overall, authorities said that the “vast majority of individuals” had demonstrated peacefully on Saturday, according to BFMTV.
Posting on X, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of the far-left La France Insoumise Party, emphasized that the majority of demonstrators on Sunday had made their point peacefully. “While news channels are flooded with images of violence in dozens of cities, everything is unfolding peacefully with tens of thousands of people calmly mobilized. Two worlds, two realities.”
Youth activists also led solidarity protests in Belgium, Albania and Italy , where police arrested more than 70 people for identification in the city of Milan on Sunday, according to CNN affiliate SkyTG24.
Reuters reported Sunday that police in Milan clashed with stone-throwing demonstrators for a second day, with law enforcement firing tear gas and water cannons in response. SkyTG24 shared video from a supermarket in Milan, showing the windows smashed out and merchandise scattered over the floor after looting.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni condemned the looting in a statement posted on social media, and said that she will convene a meeting in Rome on Monday to “evaluate further measures against those who exploit legitimate demonstrations to sow violence and chaos.”
The wave of protests in France has its roots in the country’s public school system. Earlier this fall, French high school students organized scattered protests demanding reduced class sizes, increased spending on teachers, investments in infrastructure designed to withstand the climate crisis and an end to police violence against young people.
In the past decade and a half, a rise in fertility coupled with funding cuts has led to more students, but fewer teachers in classrooms. The French Education Minister Edouard Geffray has met with student protesters multiple times in recent weeks, although an agreement is yet to be made.
This story has been updated with additional information.
CNN’s Eline Baudier Kim, Chandler Thornton, Sharon Braithwaite and Max Saltman contributed reporting.

articles.title_zh: Jet skids off runway after botched takeoff at Las Vegas airport
articles.content_orig:
A private jet aborted its takeoff after it ran off the end of a runway at Harry Reid International Airport Sunday morning.
The aircraft, a Dassault Falcon 50 with tail number N200SG, was departing from Runway 1L at about 11 a.m. when it skidded off the runway and made contact with the airport’s perimeter fence.
“At approximately 11 a.m., upon departure, a general aviation aircraft skid off runway 1L at LAS and made contact with the perimeter fence. There are no known injuries at this time,” the airport said.
“Runways 1R and 1L will be closed for inspection, and travelers may experience some delays. We will provide updates as more information becomes available,” authorities said.
A flight-tracking map shared on social media by Red Wave Press shows the jet moving slowly from its taxi position and turning onto the runway.
The plane then continues past the end of the pavement before veering to the right and coming to a complete stop. The airport said the aircraft made contact with the perimeter fence.
The Federal Aviation Administration has issued a ground stop for the airport, citing an “aircraft emergency.” Airport officials said the stop may result in delays and urged travelers to check with their airlines about flight status.
FAA registry records show that the aircraft, a three-engine business jet, is owned by Jacks Wings LLC of Boca Raton, Florida.

articles.title_zh: Emmanuel Macron faces political firestorm after riots
articles.content_orig:
Henry's 2023 Sarkozy-Gaddafi trial coverage was cited in the European Parliament’s anti-corruption resolution, and the French culture ministry referenced his Louvre funding analysis during its 2025 budget negotiations
On Sunday morning, the City of Love resembled a City of Hate.
Trucks and cars lay smouldering, bus shelters were smashed, and mounds of melted bins and Lime bikes littered the typically picturesque avenues and boulevards.
Most shocking were the dozens of shops where metal shutters had been prised open, window panes smashed, and stores looted to the last item.
Similar scenes of chaos had played out in Marseille, Lyon and other big cities. In Limoges, the 19th-century bell tower came crashing down in flames in an eerie reminder of the Notre-Dame blaze. This time, however, the damage was deliberate.
“It’s a war zone,” lamented Mehmet, a retired tailor of Turkish origin who has lived in Paris “since de Gaulle was still alive”. “We’re the ones who’ll end up paying for all this. It’s unacceptable. France isn’t what it used to be.”
It all started festively enough.
Parents and teachers marched with pupils and students manning carnival-like floats – a huge Trojan horse passed by my front door – as Yellow Vests and unions joined the fray to protest against rising living costs and for “social justice” .
It is arguably uplifting to seeing your children peacefully demonstrate for a better world and vent their anger at a tide of existential threats from war to climate change and AI.
It is tragic to see their genuine concerns eclipsed by mindless anarchy.
As the government has said, it was a “miracle” no one died. In fact, two did, one from a seizure during the Paris protest, a second falling from atop the Arc de Triomphe.
The police, who have been the main butt of young protesters’ fury for their alleged brutality, were completely overwhelmed and at times absent.
Benoit Payan, Marseille’s mayor, asked why he had just one company of national riot police for a city 2.5 times the area of Paris. It felt almost as if officers had vanished to teach France a lesson.
The Left and Greens called for Laurent Nunez, the interior minister, to resign.
Some foreign leaders gleefully weaponised the chaos.
“ France is burning ! The immigration of people from an entirely different world, people with hatred in their hearts, has shattered that once great country,” Donald Trump said in a post on his Truth Social platform. “Close your Borders and take control, before it is too late!”
Iran and Hungary followed suit.
Shell-shocked, Emmanuel Macron , the French president, broke his silence to issue a frankly laughable promise that all masked and black-clad looters would be “pursued and punished”.
Sebastien Lecornu, the French president’s embattled prime minister, called on the French to choose sides between “the Republic or the rioters”.
But it was another political choice that was on most French people’s minds.
Mr Macron has only six months left in the Elysée Palace before his second and final presidential term ends.
One wonders whether such a fractured country has the patience to wait that long to choose his replacement.
While France, and the wider world, waits to see if the country jolts to the Right or Left, it is unlikely that whoever takes the reins in April will be as equivocal as the incumbent leader.
The French president addressed the nation on Sunday night, saying that public gatherings would be banned to halt rioting if necessary.
He pledged that there would be harsh consequences for the “criminals” who were looting and burning, and said they must “never” be confused with the peaceful protesters. “They will answer for what they have done to the Republic,” he added.
But the current revolt has stripped the 48-year-old centrist of his last fig leaf of domestic political capital since his disastrous decision to call snap elections in 2024.
In the ensuing period, France has lurched like a headless cockerel from one domestic crisis to another, run by a minority government barely able to pass a budget.
With the costs of the riots running into the “hundreds of millions” and the state more cash-strapped than ever, the age-old Gallic reflex of whipping out the cheque book to quell unrest – such as during the 2018 Yellow Vest revolt – is no longer an option.
In its defence, the French government plaintively asserts that education spending has risen during the Macron presidency, including by around 5 per cent in real terms since 2019. It is proposing a further €1.2bn (£1bn) increase next year.
However, it also plans to abolish almost 1,600 permanent teaching posts, while pension costs consume nearly a third of the education ministry’s budget. Universities have fared worse, with funding per student falling sharply since Mr Macron took office.
But even if the government could stump up more cash, the demands are now so diffuse that forking out more is unlikely to make much difference.
Deprived of the normal levers, Mr Lecornu pointed the finger squarely at the “extreme Left”, saying it was no coincidence that groups had targeted “centres of power” on Saturday. Many protesters took up social media calls to storm the parliament and the Elysée Palace – to no avail.
“Clearly this is a political manoeuvre,” Mr Lecornu claimed.
The unnamed culprit is Jean-Luc Mélenchon , firebrand leader of the Leftist France Unbowed.
Polls suggest the 75-year-old putative revolutionary could reach the presidential run-off against the National Rally’s Marine Le Pen next May – even if the latest place him on a par with Raphael Glucksmann, the Socialist, and Edouard Philippe, the centre-Right former prime minister.
Mr Mélenchon has shamelessly blown hot and cold, accusing the government and police of being the cause of all the damage before issuing a late-night call for calm, almost as an afterthought. In his defence, many pupils and students say he is the only one who has stuck up for them.
The Le Pen camp, meanwhile, hopes to capitalise on the unrest with a pledge to restore order.
Ms Le Pen said the troubles showed that Mr Macron’s administration was “running on fumes, exhausted and disoriented”.
“We are experiencing a profound crisis of trust and authority, which poses a threat to democracy,” said Ms Le Pen, who leads opinion polls ahead of the election.
Commentators point to the May 1968 mass protests that Charles de Gaulle decried as “la chienlit” (bed defecation, in other words, bedlam). In their wake, the French Right won a huge parliamentary majority.
“Macron’s 10 years end in absolute chaos. The Left is guilty, Macronistes are accomplices. Vote!” headlined RN spin doctors in a social media edit of the worst of the violence.
Mr Macron may be a busted flush. But to claim Mr Mélenchon – who is gunning for young voters and the high-immigrant banlieues – is somehow controlling this mayhem is fanciful. He is merely fanning the flames of a far wider anger smouldering in this combustible and divided nation.
As one editorialist put it: “The chaos in the streets reflects the chaos in [French] heads.”
The question is whether any presidential candidate is in a position to address it.

articles.title_orig: China looks like it's dumping Treasury debt but may actually be stashing it in Canada and Belgium
articles.title_zh: China looks like it's dumping Treasury debt but may actually be stashing it in Canada and Belgium
articles.content_orig:
China was once the top holder of U.S. Treasuries but has been shedding its massive stockpile for years, fueling fears of de-dollarization, but official data may not fully capture Beijing’s actual portfolio.
The decline began in earnest around 2021, but as recently as April 2022, China still held $1 trillion in Treasury securities. U.S. data on Friday show that’s been whittled down to just $591 billion as of August, the lowest in 18 years and down from $700 billion a year earlier.
But the data is collected primarily from U.S.-based custodians and broker-dealers, according to the Treasury Department, which adds that U.S. securities held in overseas custody accounts may not be attributed to the actual owners.
As a result, China watchers have long been skeptical of a wholesale dumping of U.S. assets, pointing to suspicious jumps in Treasury holdings elsewhere that coincide with the steep Chinese drop.
Canada’s holdings soared to $465 billion in August from just $169 billion in the same month five years ago . Similarly, Belgium’s stockpile shot up to $490.5 billion from $228 billion over the same span. After including other bonds backed by federal housing agencies, the numbers are even more staggering.
To be sure, China has been challenging the U.S. for supremacy in global finance, seeking to unseat the dollar as the world’s top currency.
U.S. sanctions against Russia after its 2022 invasion of Ukraine further encouraged the People’s Bank of China and other central banks around the world to diversify away from dollar reserves and toward alternative assets like gold.
President Donald Trump’s trade war, which has been particularly focused on China, gave Beijing more reasons to ditch Treasuries and decouple from the U.S.
But at the same time, China has relied more heavily on export-led growth in recent years as domestic demand remains stagnant amid the festering property crash and debt hangover.
So despite the friction with the U.S. and other trade partners, China posted a $1.2 trillion trade surplus in 2025—the largest in recorded history—growing three times faster than global goods trade.
This year looks to break that record. For the first nine months of 2026, China’s trade surplus reached $938 billion , with expectations growing that it could surpass last year’s milestone.
Such massive surpluses must be recycled back somewhere, perhaps leading China to shift its Treasury debt to non-U.S. custodian banks in other countries—and not show up as “China” in official U.S. data.
“The evidence that China uses a Canadian custodian for some of its Agencies is especially strong — note the sudden jump in Canada’s holdings and the big impact of the detailed June survey at some early points,” Brad Setser, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations and a former Treasury official, posted on X on Wednesday while highlighting a Bloomberg story on the subject.
In May, he wrote a deep dive into China’s holdings. Since about 2020, there’s been a huge increase in Treasuries held in custodians in the United Kingdom, France, Luxembourg, and Belgium.
Adding up China’s holdings with those in Canada and the European custodial centers results in a total as high as $500 billion. Even an adjustment that looks only at Canada, Luxembourg, and France since about 2022 puts China’s holdings at around $300 billion.
While China has reduced its stash of long-term Treasuries and increased short-term bills, Setser estimated that China’s total U.S. financial holdings remain between 50% and 55% of its reserve portfolio.
“Both the Treasury and the Agency portfolios need to be adjusted for the bonds that China keeps on custody in Canada and in Europe,” he said. “That adds to uncertainty around the estimate, as it seems likely that China is now using multiple non-U.S. custodians to mask its true holdings.”

articles.title_orig: France’s riots are the death throes of Macronism
articles.title_zh: France’s riots are the death throes of Macronism
articles.content_orig:
On Sunday morning, the City of Love resembled a City of Hate.
Trucks and cars lay smouldering, bus shelters were smashed, and mounds of melted bins and Lime bikes littered the typically picturesque avenues and boulevards.
Most shocking were the dozens of shops where metal shutters had been prised open, window panes smashed, and stores looted to the last item.
Similar scenes of chaos had played out in Marseille, Lyon and other big cities. In Limoges, the 19th-century bell tower came crashing down in flames in an eerie reminder of the Notre-Dame blaze. This time, however, the damage was deliberate.
"It's a war zone," lamented Mehmet, a retired tailor of Turkish origin who has lived in Paris "since de Gaulle was still alive". "We're the ones who'll end up paying for all this. It's unacceptable. France isn't what it used to be."
Destruction on the streets of Paris a day after national protests - Reuters/Benoit Tessier
It all started festively enough.
Parents and teachers marched with pupils and students manning carnival-like floats – a huge Trojan horse passed by my front door – as Yellow Vests and unions joined the fray to protest against rising living costs and for "social justice" .
It is arguably uplifting to seeing your children peacefully demonstrate for a better world and vent their anger at a tide of existential threats from war to climate change and AI.
It is tragic to see their genuine concerns eclipsed by mindless anarchy.
As the government has said, it was a "miracle" no one died. In fact, two did, one from a seizure during the Paris protest, a second falling from atop the Arc de Triomphe.
The police, who have been the main butt of young protesters' fury for their alleged brutality, were completely overwhelmed and at times absent.
Benoit Payan, Marseille's mayor, asked why he had just one company of national riot police for a city 2.5 times the area of Paris. It felt almost as if officers had vanished to teach France a lesson.
The Left and Greens called for Laurent Nunez, the interior minister, to resign.
Boutiques, banks and independent shops were looted during the protests - The Press Association/Lucy North
Some foreign leaders gleefully weaponised the chaos.
" France is burning ! The immigration of people from an entirely different world, people with hatred in their hearts, has shattered that once great country," Donald Trump said in a post on his Truth Social platform. "Close your Borders and take control, before it is too late!"
Iran and Hungary followed suit.
A protester waving a French flag walks past a fire during protests in Marseille - AFP via Getty Images/THIBAUD MORITZ
Shell-shocked, Emmanuel Macron , the French president, broke his silence to issue a frankly laughable promise that all masked and black-clad looters would be "pursued and punished".
Sebastien Lecornu, the French president's embattled prime minister, called on the French to choose sides between "the Republic or the rioters".
But it was another political choice that was on most French people's minds.
Mr Macron has only six months left in the Elysée Palace before his second and final presidential term ends.
One wonders whether such a fractured country has the patience to wait that long to choose his replacement.
While France, and the wider world, waits to see if the country jolts to the Right or Left, it is unlikely that whoever takes the reins in April will be as equivocal as the incumbent leader.
The French president addressed the nation on Sunday night, saying that public gatherings would be banned to halt rioting if necessary.
He pledged that there would be harsh consequences for the "criminals" who were looting and burning, and said they must "never" be confused with the peaceful protesters. "They will answer for what they have done to the Republic," he added.
But the current revolt has stripped the 48-year-old centrist of his last fig leaf of domestic political capital since his disastrous decision to call snap elections in 2024.
In the ensuing period, France has lurched like a headless cockerel from one domestic crisis to another, run by a minority government barely able to pass a budget.
The city hall in Limoges was destroyed by fire during protests - AFP via Getty Images/PASCAL LACHENAUD
With the costs of the riots running into the "hundreds of millions" and the state more cash-strapped than ever, the age-old Gallic reflex of whipping out the cheque book to quell unrest – such as during the 2018 Yellow Vest revolt – is no longer an option.
In its defence, the French government plaintively asserts that education spending has risen during the Macron presidency, including by around 5 per cent in real terms since 2019. It is proposing a further €1.2bn (£1bn) increase next year.
However, it also plans to abolish almost 1,600 permanent teaching posts, while pension costs consume nearly a third of the education ministry's budget. Universities have fared worse, with funding per student falling sharply since Mr Macron took office.
But even if the government could stump up more cash, the demands are now so diffuse that forking out more is unlikely to make much difference.
French riot police clashed with protesters in Paris on Saturday - Reuters/Abdul Saboor
Deprived of the normal levers, Mr Lecornu pointed the finger squarely at the "extreme Left", saying it was no coincidence that groups had targeted "centres of power" on Saturday. Many protesters took up social media calls to storm the parliament and the Elysée Palace – to no avail.
"Clearly this is a political manoeuvre," Mr Lecornu claimed.
The unnamed culprit is Jean-Luc Mélenchon , firebrand leader of the Leftist France Unbowed.
Polls suggest the 75-year-old putative revolutionary could reach the presidential run-off against the National Rally's Marine Le Pen next May – even if the latest place him on a par with Raphael Glucksmann, the Socialist, and Edouard Philippe, the centre-Right former prime minister.
Mr Mélenchon has shamelessly blown hot and cold, accusing the government and police of being the cause of all the damage before issuing a late-night call for calm, almost as an afterthought. In his defence, many pupils and students say he is the only one who has stuck up for them.
A Marseille street covered in debris a day after nationwide protests against the high cost of living - AFP via Getty Images/Thibaud MORITZ
The Le Pen camp, meanwhile, hopes to capitalise on the unrest with a pledge to restore order.
Ms Le Pen said the troubles showed that Mr Macron's administration was "running on fumes, exhausted and disoriented".
"We are experiencing a profound crisis of trust and authority, which poses a threat to democracy," said Ms Le Pen, who leads opinion polls ahead of the election.
Commentators point to the May 1968 mass protests that Charles de Gaulle decried as "la chienlit" (bed defecation, in other words, bedlam). In their wake, the French Right won a huge parliamentary majority.
"Macron's 10 years end in absolute chaos. The Left is guilty, Macronistes are accomplices. Vote!" headlined RN spin doctors in a social media edit of the worst of the violence.
Mr Macron may be a busted flush. But to claim Mr Mélenchon – who is gunning for young voters and the high-immigrant banlieues – is somehow controlling this mayhem is fanciful. He is merely fanning the flames of a far wider anger smouldering in this combustible and divided nation.
As one editorialist put it: "The chaos in the streets reflects the chaos in [French] heads."
The question is whether any presidential candidate is in a position to address it.

articles.title_orig: ‘Hybrid warfare’: Taiwan drives away 16 Chinese ships
articles.title_zh: ‘Hybrid warfare’: Taiwan drives away 16 Chinese ships
articles.content_orig:
Taiwan has confronted and driven away 16 Chinese coastguard, research and fishing vessels that it said were involved in simultaneous “maritime harassment” operations.
An “unusually large” number of Chinese vessels took part in coordinated operations around Taiwan’s main island and Pratas (also known as Dongsha), a disputed island to the southwest, the Taiwanese coastguard said in a statement on Sunday.
The Chinese vessels included four fishing boats, which engaged in “simultaneous operations’ that the coastguard described as “hybrid warfare”.
Taiwan’s coastguard said its vessels took “forceful action immediately to effectively neutralise the threats” and accused Beijing of “attempting to unilaterally alter the status quo” in the Taiwan Strait and give the “false impression of jurisdiction”.
Some of the vessels reportedly entered Taiwan’s restricted waters.
Beijing claims Taiwan and Pratas as part of its territory and asserts jurisdiction over the surrounding waters, which Taipei rejects. China has long threatened to use force to regain control of Taiwan.
In an incident on October 1 , Taiwan’s coastguard fired water cannon at a Chinese recreational fishing vessel near Pratas island between Taiwan and mainland China that Beijing claims.
China has intensified its maritime pressure on Taiwan in recent months. Beijing deployed a record 244 coastguard, scientific research and other ships around Taiwan’s main island in July, Taiwanese official data show, compared with just 58 in the same month last year.
In the first 21 days of August, 152 vessels were detected; most were from the Chinese Coastguard, but fishing boats and research vessels were also involved.
China also deploys warships around Taiwan on a near-daily basis, but those are counted separately.
